#833. Tuchel and England must learn lessons of history, Seville and Southgateism | Barney Ronay

Another 3-2 win in Spain brings the lure of a golden new hyper-future – but it did not pan out that way last time

I may have the body of a weak and feeble German, but I have the heart and stomach of a manager of England. And I think it foul scorn that Spain should dare to invade the borders of my realm. Or, for that matter, any one of 24 qualified teams for Euro 2028, because at the end of the day there are no easy games at this level, I’ve always said that.

The words, there, of Thomas Tuchel, England’s Faerie King, speaking to TalkSport shortly after the glorious 3-2 defeat of the Spanish possession armada at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid.

OK, Tuchel didn’t technically say any of this. He was instead wry and spiky. He made a joke about people moaning about his team on the radio, which just goes to show he’s a good lad and one of us (disclaimer: when he wins). But this is England. And beating Spain can do some strange things to you.

Not just because Spain are the defining team of the past 20 years, six-time international trophy winners and current world and European champions. But because Spanish football culture is the global template for tone, texture and tactics, the ultimate source of the Football Association’s slightly dog‑eared footballing blueprint.

Beating Spain is like beating your super-smart but slightly controlling younger brother. It’s getting one over on that other way of playing, punitive high technique, death by possession, patience over urgency. Even better, Tuchel’s team did so in Madrid with a performance based around the hard‑running physicality that English football sees as part of its deep sporting soul.

As such it will be tempting to see this Nations League victory as a springboard, a Rubicon crossed, a shattering of the Iberian ceiling. With some justification; England have the talent to win a home European Championship two years from now. But it feels just a little bit easier to visualise now.

There was something new in seeing Spain not just outmuscled but outplayed in the first half, reduced to whinging about fouls, unable to take the ball away. Not only because England’s pressing was smart and relentless but because of the players’ ability to keep possession in tight spaces.

It is also true that a quick glance back at recent history tells us exactly how much of a golden dawn a win such as this can be. Which is: zero, zilch, nothing. No golden dawn at all.

In reality there are no Rubicon moments, no decisive levellings-up, only staging posts and warning signs, even in victory. This is the most important point about a night such as this. It won’t tell you where you’ll end up. But it may tell you how to keep heading the right way, if you’re ready to learn from recent history.

As it happens, recent history is in the room with us right now, clearing its throat, rattling its chains, trying to shift the Ouija-board dial. Here is an interesting fact. Spain have only twice conceded three goals at home in a competitive men’s international. The second time was on Sunday night, when England won 3-2 in Madrid after going 3-0 up. And the first time was 15 October 2018 when England beat Spain 3-2 in Seville after going 3-0 up.

The parallels between those games are numerically improbable. At the time of win No 1 Gareth Southgate had been in permanent charge for 684 days and one narrow World Cup semi-final defeat. Spain was his 29th game. At the time of win No 2 Tuchel had been in charge for 683 days and another narrow World Cup semi-final defeat. Spain was Tuchel’s 28th game.

That Southgate moment was greeted with understandable optimism. You know the kind of language used because it’s out here now, too. New dawns. Statement victories. Rise of a Golden Generation. Not just a benchmark but a springboard as well, an astonishing feat of carpentry if true.

So was it that? Answer: no. In fact Seville 2018 was arguably the moment Southgate-ism reached a stylistic ceiling. England played a fast-paced game of counterattack that night. The team was an attacking mix, a midfield of Winks‑Barkley‑Dier, with Sterling‑Kane‑Rashford in front. England scored 27 goals in six games the following autumn, starting most with a back four and a double pivot, ending 2019 with a 6-0, a 7-0 and a 4-0. This felt like something new.

The Covid break pretty much killed that mini-era. Or rather, it was allowed to kill it, because coaches have choices too. England went 42 weeks without a game. By November 2020 they were losing 2-0 in Belgium with a back five and a deep defensive midfield.

The Euros had already been postponed for a year. In the summer of 2021 England started the final against Italy with another back five plus Declan Rice and Kalvin Phillips, and congealed into a kind of footballing rice pudding as the game reached its crisis point.

Here is an unprovable counterfactual. If football had rolled on, if England had not had an empty year to look down and get scared, they might have retained enough momentum to go harder against Italy in that final and win it.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

But then, the Southgate era was gruelling for many of those players. There is a separate study to be made of the way so many key early Garethistas disappeared or entered a slow decline. That October 2018 team turned out to be a pop‑up thing of shifting parts, evidence of the complex, zigzagging nature of team building.

The would-be golden generation included Ben Chilwell, Eric Dier, Joe Gomez, Ross Barkley, Harry Winks and Marcus Rashford. Nathaniel Chalobah made his only appearance as a sub in added time, and still has the second-shortest England career, after Martin Kelly.

Rather than a golden dawn of ultimate glory, England entered a more talent-appropriate era of losing late-stage games against good opponents. If anything the Spain victory added to the ambient pressure around those tournaments, helping to create the sense it is now unthinkable for England to lose, because we have an image of them as winners, and English winning is the best winning, the only real winning.

The lesson remains the same now, the need to avoid both portents of doom and the lure of a golden new hyper-future. In this sense Tuchel is encouragingly restless both in defeat and victory. Even his new-season touchline look – tailored, sombre, all black – has an agreeably priestly, hair‑shirt energy; less Elizabeth I, author of the introductory quote above, more Martin Luther on his way to a business meeting in an out‑of‑town spa hotel.

Tuchel’s best quality is his obsession with analysis and objectivity. On Sunday night he was already talking about the need to improve. This can be an obstacle at times (see: process-based Argentina substitutes). But it is also a rejection of complacency, ornament, frippery. This England are better than their 2018 equivalent. That team had seven players from Leicester and Arsenal. This one has key parts from Real Madrid, Barcelona and Bayern Munich, including the current Ballon d’Or winner and a £300m midfield tripod.

The balance of the attack in Madrid was good, not just the most seductively talented players but the best parts for the plan. Anthony Gordon is an interesting figure in this respect, an intelligent, culturally adaptable, tactically aware footballer, whose game is nonetheless basically running up and down. Elite teams seem to have a place for this role now. Flank-scurry energy node. Right-sided gallop unit. Lewis Hall was also very good again. Any team looks better with a genuine left‑footed full-back, like hanging a picture straight on the wall.

Mainly what Tuchel did in Spain was to select a team with no indulgences, full commitment to a tailored gameplan, no celebrity passengers. And that style is not fixed. See also: Trent Alexander-Arnold against Croatia, and some excellent passes against a deep block even on a middling night. Stick that behind your ear as well, Thomas.

Teams are hugely complex things. Tuchel had to get to know his players. The idea you can simply bolt on an elite manager and expect instant progress was always a bit silly. No dips or lulls, no adaptation. This might work if you come from the same cultural system. But plonking on a brain from someone else’s body is still a way of looking for shortcuts, the managerial equivalent of sticking it in the mixer and hoping for the best. There you go. Give us a final fix on 75 years of inherited domestic culture.

Tuchel is now a little further along with all this. He even did the backs-to-the-wall thing better, waiting to the last moment to press the defensive emergency button, the sight of Dan Burn rumbling out a signal to both teams that this really is the end of the night, like turning on all the lights and getting the DJ to play Don’t Look Back in Anger.

Max Dowman (pictured) became England Under-21s’ youngest-ever goalscorer by grabbing the late winner in a 3-2 friendly victory over France at Ashton Gate.

Lee Carsley’s side made a lightning start as Tottenham's Mikey Moore gave England an early lead on his first under-21s start. Divin Mubama doubled their lead with a header as Ethan Nwaneri set up both of the hosts' first-half goals.

The Young Lions looked comfortable but Tommy Setford allowed France to pull a goal back after he let Giovani Versini’s cross slip through his fingers. The French winger equalised in style moments later, scoring with a shot from distance.

Carsley had handed a first start to promising Arsenal youngster Dowman and he proved to be the hero, tapping in from Harrison Armstrong's pass to give England the win at only 16 years old. Press Association

Sunday night was a wonderful game. It was England’s most complete performance under Tuchel. But the lesson hasn’t changed. Trust the process, not the results. Keep doing the ruthless, adaptive things that got you there. England will at some point have to beat the best. And the Nations League is a very useful tool. Win it next summer and taking that final step starts to look a whole lot less of an Arthurian fever dream.

This Vampire Survivors spin-off has a lot of love for the famous grimdark sci-fi universe, but without the intimidatingly dense lore and complex systems.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We've had no shortage of great Warhammer 40K games lately, but most aren't exactly aimed at the casual crowd. Warhammer Survivors changes that, finally providing curious gamers with an easy entry point into the grim darkness of the 41st millennium.

Developed by Auroch Digital (in collaboration with Vampire Survivors' Poncle), this new spin on the survivors-like roguelite subgenre mixes the sci-fi 40,000 setting with the pure fantasy Age of Sigmar universe. This means heroes and enemies from all over the Warhammer mythos meet together in a bite-sized game that anyone can figure out and enjoy in less than five minutes.

When you look at the alternatives, that's a remarkable achievement for a franchise that's notoriously hard (and often expensive) to get into.

Warhammer Survivors isn't bogged down by dense lore, involved mechanics, or massive campaign playthroughs. It's more of an "inspired by" effort that gives casuals a small taste of the series' iconic characters — including Boltgun's Malum Caedo — and factions like the terrifying Tyranids, the raucous Orks, and the foul forces of Chaos.

All of 40K's (and Age of Sigmar's) recognizable elements are on display, but they serve more as flavoring sprinkled on top of Vampire Survivors' successful formula.

If you're new to the Survivors-like subgenre, it's a unique gaming experience. You battle an endless onslaught of enemies that slowly march towards you, with your character passively attacking automatically. You only need to move them around sprawling arenas and select level-up upgrades and items after collecting enough gems (skulls in this case).

The moment-to-moment gameplay is as simple as it can get outside of walking sims and interactive "experiences," but there's a deceiving depth to item synergies and how to correctly "build" characters to endure all the carnage.

Unlike Poncle's original game, Warhammer Survivors struggles a bit to get going. The early hours are sluggish until you unlock certain meta upgrades, but its still got that Vampire Survivors magic at its core.

As far as "podcast/gym games" go, this is a perfect fit. There's just enough going on to keep one's brain engaged, but minimal inputs and a tight overarching design lead to a rhythm that's easy to get into without using much brainpower. It's oddly satisfying to weave through enemies and level up your firepower, watching a single Astra Militarum grunt grow into a full Lasgun-spamming, chainsword-wielding wrecking ball.

Achievement and unlock hunters will find enough to bite into here, too. It's unclear if the devs will continue to add more Warhammer 40K and Age of Sigmar deep cuts to this game via DLCs and free updates, but those universes have daunting depths to explore. This really could become a gateway game for future 40K fans: by the time they realize they're hooked, they'll already have 2000 pts of space marines painted and ready to play.

As massive sci-fi and fantasy properties try to aggressively expand and absorb more and more fans, it's easy to pander to already-converted diehards too much. And sure, we can't wait for strategy heavyweights like Dawn of War 4 and Total War: WH40K either, but they're hardly good recommendations for folks who don't even know what a Space Marine is or why the robotic Necrons are so grumpy.

Warhammer Survivors won't answer those questions beyond the surface-level iconography, but it's fun enough to push those curious to dig deeper and embrace the same material in more mature video game genres... and maybe even pick up a few miniatures.

Warhammer Survivors is now available on PC (Steam & GOG), PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch 1/2, and mobile (iOS & Android). It's also playable on Game Pass.

Fran Ruiz is our resident Star Wars guy. His hunger for movies and TV series is only matched by his love for video games. He got a BA of English Studies, focusing on English Literature, from the University of Malaga, in Spain, as well as a Master's Degree in English Studies, Multilingual and Intercultural Communication. On top of writing features and other longform articles for Space.com since 2021, he is a frequent collaborator of VG247 and other gaming sites. He also serves as associate editor over at Star Wars News Net and its sister site, Movie News Net.

#831. Robertson eclipses Dalglish to become Scotland's most capped man

You've done Liverpool and Scotland proud - Kenny Dalglish on Andy Robertson's career

Andy Robertson has become Scotland's most capped men's international after starting in Monday's Nations League defeat in Switzerland to reach 103 appearances for his country.

Twelve years on from his debut - off the bench in a Poland friendly - he surpassed his friend and fellow Liverpool legend, Kenny Dalglish, whose record haul had stood for 40 years.

After moving level with the man they - and he - will always call King, the Tottenham Hotspur left-back shifted chat towards the former forward, his commendable humility laid bare.

But, in St Gallen, the spotlight shone on one of Scotland's favourite sons as he moves solo at the summit, even if the scoreline was a disappointment.

Robertson set to make history, but hero Dalglish will always be King

Inside the fairytale journey of Scotland captain Robertson

Andy Robertson on his hero, Kenny Dalglish

For much of this year, Dalglish was the only man to have pulled on the navy blue of Scotland more times than Robertson.

'King Kenny' topped the list on 102 caps - earning his last in November 1986 against Luxembourg when in a player-manager role at Liverpool.

Few since have even come close to toppling him - and Robertson is keen to stress the throne is still reserved for Dalglish - but it is perhaps fitting it is the current captain, given their great friendship.

Which allows Dalglish to say he's not having any of it.

"He always says: 'You've got millions more games. Nations League, what's that? They didn't have that in my day!'" Robertson joked on the Stick to Football podcast recently.

"I think he might bring up a ratio for years-to-games-played so he's still on top.

"It's obviously something that's been on my radar for a while now. When you get to 80-odd caps, you start to look up."

Dalglish can console himself that his record of 30 goals - held jointly with Denis Law - is safely out of Robertson's reach.

But not out of John McGinn's - the midfielder's double against North Macedonia on Friday took him to within six of the legendary duo.

The Aston Villa captain is lurking only eight caps behind Robertson on the all-time caps list, too, so the Scotland men's centurion club could have three members soon.

Since being given the armband by Alex McLeish after Scott Brown retired in 2018, Robertson has captained Scotland 33 times more than any other player.

At the time, he had earned just 22 caps and was just 24 but had established himself as Liverpool's left-back as they reached the Champions League final.

Now he is the only man to have led Scotland out at three major finals, reaching the milestone at the World Cup this summer.

Scotland and Napoli midfielder Scott McTominay enthused: "He's such a great captain and he's got that good balance between being one of the senior players and saying you need to wake up if you're not playing well.

"Then he's also got the personable side, organising things with the manager, helping young players and stuff. He's brilliant with that, brilliant."

One of those young players is 20-year-old Findlay Curtis, who told the media the night before Robertson's historic night that his captain has "probably been the biggest role model" he's looked up to since joining the international set-up earlier this year.

Perhaps that was because Robertson did him a turn back in the day. Unbeknownst to the skipper.

Rangers winger Curtis was only 14 during the Covid pandemic and was partial to playing a bit of Fifa, and Robertson was a star in his team.

"I was just thinking, I had him in my Fifa team," he explained. "[For] defending and he was just fast as well.

"What a servant he has been for the country."

'I had him in my Fifa team!' - Findlay Curtis on going from fan to team-mate of Robertson

Robertson has played under four permanent Scotland team bosses in his 12-year international career.

It was Strachan who plucked him from the under-21s to hand him his debut as a 19-year-old in a win over Poland in March 2014.

McLeish made him captain in 2018, calling Robertson the "outstanding candidate" and an "inspirational figure" - and now he has played five times for new boss Sebastien Pocognoli.

He even played one game under interim manager Malky Mackay in a friendly against the Netherlands at Pittodrie in 2017 as the Scottish FA searched for Strachan's replacement.

However, it is Steve Clarke's seven-year stint that Robertson will be mainly associated with, as the pair led Scotland to three major tournaments.

Robertson played 68 times for Clarke, all of them as captain, and the recently departed head coach consistently praised his figurehead.

"He's been a fantastic captain for Scotland," Clarke said at the World Cup.

"He's worked ever so hard for the country and he leads the group like the leader he is - and he's very, very important to me and the squad."

Over the piece, Robertson's caps are spread fairly evenly among friendlies and qualification games.

Crucially, though, he has also played nine times in major tournaments. What will rankle with him is there is only one win among those nine - June's victory over Haiti in Boston at the World Cup.

Overall, though, Robertson's Scotland career can be characterised by consistency.

He has started 101 of his 103 caps, rarely ever being substituted. He has not missed a camp in three years.

The only question seems to be how many Scotland caps will Robertson end up with?

At 32 and still playing in the Premier League, it appears there will be plenty more to come.

“I feel like I’m so sad about my dad and Mark," she shared, "that I don’t notice physical pain."

And her health has only complicated her grief journey. Glanville added that she feels "some guilt" after missing Hasche's funeral because she has "so much fluid" in her head.

At a 2013 brain scan, she learned a growth "doubled in size" and that she needed surgery again."When they woke me, I was screaming in pain," she wrote. "The procedure had failed. I had a massive bleed and the doctors made it plain that my chances of surviving were precarious if they didn’t operate again. This time they needed to access my brain in the old-fashioned way—through my skull."Thankfully, Emilia shared, she's now "at a hundred per cent."

SpaceX's Starship megarocket is slated to launch on its ambitious 15th flight test as soon as this Friday (Nov. 13). Will you be able to spot its leviathan upper stage, known as Ship, or its Starlink satellite passengers as they circle Earth during the historic orbital jaunt?

Flight 15's 75-minute launch window opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT) on Nov. 13. Starship will fly from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas, where it will be 4:45 p.m. at the opening of the window — about an hour before sunset. The launch could therefore be especially dramatic for folks in the area.

"As it launches towards the southeast, and it will be daylight, then the prospects for viewing from the U.S. are going to be in Texas and the states along the Gulf of Mexico," Robert Massey, deputy executive director at the Royal Astronomical Society, told Space.com. "They could see the exhaust plume (the 'jellyfish') with the sky darker for observers further east."

If all goes to plan, Starship's Super Heavy booster will propel the Ship upper stage through the densest part of Earth's atmosphere before returning to Starbase for a powered landing and capture via the "chopstick" arms of the "Mechazilla" tower system. Ship, meanwhile, will go on to orbit Earth approximately 14 times over the following 22 hours, during which time it will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites before returning to Starbase for its own ambitious catch attempt.

Satellite visibility in the night sky depends on a cocktail of factors, from the size of the spacecraft to its reflectivity, orbital inclination and position relative to the Earth and sun.

Ship is big — about 171 feet (52 meters) tall — so it will be a viable target for skywatchers, experts say.

"It certainly will be visible in twilight hours. It should be very bright, considerably brighter than the Starlink satellites due to its size," professor James Osborn of Durham University told Space.com. "Where and when is a bit more tricky."

Ship and its Starlink satellites may be seen in the 90 minutes directly after sunset on Nov. 13 and before sunrise on Nov. 14, as the probes catch the sunlight on either side of Earth's colossal shadow as they drift through the twilight sky.

The spacecraft will initially appear as a string of bright, evenly spaced lights, with Ship most likely appearing significantly brighter than the Starlink satellites. However, Osborn noted that the lack of publicly available data makes it challenging to forecast exactly when the spacecraft will appear.

"During its 14 orbits over 22 hours, the spacecraft is between inclinations of 30.5 [degrees] N and S of the equator," explained Massey. "So it will be best viewed between those latitudes, and then lower in the sky up to latitudes of 40 N and 40 S. That's pretty much the whole of the contiguous U.S."

Space.com skywatching columnist and veteran meteorologist Joe Rao shared further details on what stargazers may see with the naked eye as Ship drifts silently through the autumn sky.

"When it passes overhead, it will look like a bright, fast-moving star crossing the sky — similar to the International Space Station, but potentially even brighter depending on its orientation," explained Rao. "The Starlink V3 satellites are much smaller, so not as bright, perhaps ranging anywhere from 2nd to 4th magnitude, depending on the angle of illumination with reflected light from the sun."

Magnitude is the scale used by astronomers to measure the brightness of objects in the night sky. The lower the magnitude, the brighter the object! The unaided eye can make out objects with a magnitude of around +6.5 under ideal dark sky conditions, while the planet Venus currently shines at magnitude -4.41.

The Starlink train will likely fall further behind Starship as the 22-hour mission progresses, while the train itself will become more elongated, according to Rao. "For locations where it will make a high arc across the sky, the Starship should be visible for at least a few minutes, although because it is orbiting at a lower altitude (170 miles/275 km) compared to the ISS, it probably will appear to move somewhat faster. "

There are multiple handy resources that should allow you to track Ship and the newly deployed batch of V3 Starlink satellites following their scheduled launch on Nov. 13, including the websites Heavens-Above, Star Dash, Orbital Radar and Find Starlink.

Be sure to keep an eye on our Starship Flight 15 live blog for all the latest news along with our launch timings article containing details on how to watch SpaceX's potentially historic orbital launch attempt.

Editor's Note: If you capture a photo of Starship and want to share it with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

Anthony Wood joined Space.com in April 2025 after contributing articles to outlets including IGN, New Atlas and Gizmodo. He has a passion for the night sky, science, Hideo Kojima, and human space exploration, and can’t wait for the day when astronauts once again set foot on the moon.

#828. Wales without Williams for Portugal as Bellamy makes Vitinha point

Former Liverpool full-back Neco Williams has 67 Wales caps, scoring five goals

Wales will be without right-back Neco Williams for their final Nations League group match against reigning champions Portugal on Tuesday (19:45 GMT), while goalkeeper Karl Darlow is a doubt.

Nottingham Forest's Williams has been ruled out after he was injured during Saturday's 3-1 defeat in Norway, while Manchester United's Darlow missed training on Monday and will be assessed further.

Midfielder Ethan Ampadu will also miss out at Cardiff City Stadium because of suspension, but centre-back Ben Cabango and winger Sorba Thomas are available after serving one-match bans.

Wales will finish bottom of Group A4 whatever happens against leaders Portugal, and Craig Bellamy's side will have a relegation play-off in March against one of the League B runners-up for a place in the top tier.

"One or two players had to come off through injury [in Norway]. One or two have come through; one or two haven't," said Bellamy.

"Neco's going to be out. Darlow, we'll wait and see later, and everyone else is fully fit."

What Wales need to stay in Nations League top tier

With less riding on this fixture than there might have been, Bellamy could be tempted to make further changes to his side from the loss in Oslo.

Cardiff City attacking midfielder Rubin Colwill shone as a substitute, while Bournemouth's David Brooks came off the bench to score an excellent goal.

Colwill's performance was a particularly popular talking point among fans, many of whom have long been calling for the 24-year-old playmaker to feature more regularly for Wales.

"Rubin's been pushing [to start] for a while," said Bellamy. "Once you get this kid in the final third, then he's a player. We've just got to get him in those areas.

"But he's also got to offer us without the ball as well. If you're not good without the ball, you cannot be a top player.

"If you want a lesson tomorrow without the ball, watch Vitinha [Portugal's Paris St-Germain midfielder] if he plays.

"Rubin has moved [up a level] and long may that continue, because if it does Wales have got a brilliant player.

"I'm more harsh on Rubin because I've known him since he was so young, but credit to him and his manager at Cardiff [Brian Barry-Murphy].

"He's helping develop a real player for us that's going to hopefully have a huge impact for the next five to 10 years."

#827. Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon

Far below the ocean's surface, a constant snowfall drifts through the darkness. But unlike the frozen flakes that fall from the sky, this underwater snow consists of tiny clumps of waste, dead organisms, and other debris. Known as marine snow, these particles contain everything from mucus and animal feces to silt and the remains of microscopic plankton.

As this material sinks, it carries enormous quantities of carbon from the upper ocean toward the seafloor. Researchers estimate that marine snow removes more than 10 gigatons of carbon from surface waters each year. Yet only about two gigatons reach depths where that carbon can remain stored for hundreds or even thousands of years.

Why so much carbon fails to make it into the deep ocean has long puzzled scientists. Now, researchers from UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the University of Lincoln have identified a surprisingly important factor: how sticky the marine snow is.

Their findings, published October 8 in the journal Science, show that the viscosity, or thickness and gooeyness, of marine snow influences how quickly bacteria break it apart and how far it can sink. According to the researchers, the stickiest particles can transport more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as particles with a thinner, less viscous consistency.

Marine snow plays an important role in Earth's carbon cycle, the natural movement of carbon among the atmosphere, oceans, land, and living organisms. By transporting carbon into deep water, sinking particles can keep some of it isolated from the atmosphere for centuries or longer.

However, not every particle survives the journey. Bacteria feed on marine snow as it descends, gradually breaking down the material and affecting how much carbon reaches the ocean's depths.

The new research provides the first detailed look at how living bacteria interact with the physical structure of marine snow and, more broadly, mucus itself. These interactions are important well beyond the ocean's carbon cycle. Similar relationships between bacteria and mucus help sustain coral reefs, kelp forests, plant root systems, and the digestive systems of humans and other animals.

Until recently, scientists lacked the technology to observe these interactions at the microscopic scale needed to understand them.

A Four-Year Quest to See Inside Marine Snow

The project began in 2021, when Bryce Inman, then a postdoctoral researcher at Scripps Oceanography, set out to explore what he calls "the muscoscape."

"Observing individual bacteria interacting with the physical structure of mucus had never been possible," said Inman.

Together with colleagues including Farooq Azam, a microbiologist and professor emeritus at Scripps, Inman spent four years trying to overcome that limitation. Multiple attempts were unsuccessful before the team finally developed a working technique in 2025.

Their solution combined 3D confocal microscopy with specially designed fluorescent molecules. Confocal microscopy uses light to capture detailed images at different depths within a sample, allowing researchers to reconstruct its structure in three dimensions. The fluorescent molecules helped make features of the material visible.

For the first time, the scientists could examine the "physical terrain" of individual marine snow particles while watching how living bacteria moved through and interacted with them.

The images revealed a surprisingly intricate microscopic environment, complete with structural differences that affect where bacteria can settle and how easily they can reach the material inside.

Much like snowflakes in the atmosphere, marine snow particles vary considerably. Each contains its own mixture of organic and inorganic materials, creating differences in composition, structure, and viscosity.

The researchers' new imaging approach, described in a companion study published in Nature Communications, revealed that bacteria preferentially colonize areas near a particle's surface where the material is less viscous.

The denser, stickier regions deeper inside are much harder for bacteria to penetrate.

"Bacteria can latch on to less viscous portions of each particle, but cannot reach more viscous regions until they break it down," said Inman. "Think of it like a worm in an apple: the flesh is easy to penetrate, but the core is tough to chew through"

This difference has important consequences for how long marine snow remains intact.

In laboratory experiments, the scientists observed that particles with greater viscosity resisted bacterial degradation and fragmentation for longer periods. Computer simulations further suggested that these stickier particles can descend to greater depths before breaking apart.

Based on these results, the team estimates that highly viscous marine snow can deliver more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as less viscous particles.

The findings help explain why some sinking material transports carbon much farther into the ocean than other particles, even though both begin their journeys near the surface.

"How far marine snow can sink is a surprisingly complicated problem, and we have added another - very gooey - piece to the puzzle," said Inman.

A Discovery With Implications Beyond the Ocean

Although the research focuses on marine snow, its implications extend to many environments where bacteria interact with mucus.

Mucus is often regarded as a relatively simple, slippery substance. But the new imaging technology reveals that it has a complex internal landscape, with microscopic structures that can influence how bacteria behave.

Understanding these physical features could help scientists investigate biological processes in settings ranging from human digestive health to the recovery of damaged coral reefs.

The method also opens opportunities to explore interactions that previously could not be observed directly, providing researchers with a new way to study the microscopic environments inhabited by bacteria.

Mucus, slime, whatever you want to call it, "has a surprising amount of structure," Inman said. "There are bulges, crevasses, all this sort of structure to it that we really had no idea about at a scale smaller than bacteria. This is the first time we're really examining this physical habitat."

The discovery adds an important missing piece to scientists' understanding of how carbon travels through the ocean. It also demonstrates that something as seemingly ordinary as the thickness of underwater slime can have far-reaching consequences for the planet's natural systems.

Additional funding for the research was provided by the Simons Foundation and the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council.

Swansea City look to be facing a fight to hold on to Vitor Matos amid serious interest in their head coach from French top-flight club Strasbourg.

Matos is under contract at Swansea until 2030, meaning the Championship side would be due significant compensation should he be lured away.

But that has not stopped Strasbourg targeting the 38-year-old Portuguese, who is due to celebrate a year in charge at Swansea later this month.

Matos' fellow countryman Hugo Oliveira is the current Strasbourg boss, but is under pressure after a run of five defeats in six matches.

Oliveira has managed only three wins in 10 league games since succeeding Gary O'Neil - who left to become Ipswich Town boss â in July.

O'Neil led Strasbourg to an eighth-place finish last season, but they are currently 13th in Ligue 1, only two points above the relegation zone.

Strasbourg are a sister club of Premier League side Chelsea.

Matos has turned Swansea from potential relegation contenders to promotion hopefuls since taking charge, with the club 20th in the Championship when he took over last November.

The Swans finished 11th last season and have made further strides in the first third of this campaign.

Vitor Matos led Swansea to seven wins in their first 10 league games of the season, though they have since lost four in five

Matos' team have been among the early-season pacesetters in the second tier, enjoying two spells on top of the table, but their form has dipped in recent weeks.

Swansea have suffered four defeats in their past five matches, though they remain only three points off top spot going into Saturday's home game against West Bromwich Albion.

Matos was touted as a contender to take charge at Crystal Palace earlier this season - the Eagles have since appointed Thomas Frank - while he has also been linked with a return to Portugal on the back of his impact with the Swans.

Latest Swansea City news, analysis and fan views

When asked in October about the Palace links, Matos said: "I'm Swansea manager. I love being here, love my players, love the staff, so my focus is always on the next game and what we can do better."

"The reality is there'll always be interest in anyone performing well in any role on and off the pitch," Gorringe said.

Philae drifted and bounced around the comet for two hours before Rosetta's cameras lost track of it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P. To say it was a bumpy landing would be an understatement.

The European Space Agency's Philae lander separated from an orbiter called Rosetta ahead of its historic landing in 2014. It was supposed to use harpoons to secure itself on to the surface of Comet 67P, but the harpoons never fired.

When it touched down, it immediately bounced back up into space. The first bounce brought Philae half a mile above the comet's surface before gravity brought it back down.

Philae was missing for almost two years before scientists found it. Images from Rosetta showed Philae stuck in a dark crevice on top of the rubber duck-shaped comet.

The European Space Agency's Rosetta and Philae expedition was a first-of-its-kind mission, an endeavour to not just rendezvous with a comet and watch it change over time as it approached the sun (that was Rosetta's job), but also to soft-land a probe on its icy and rocky surface to see what a comet is truly made of.

The Rosetta and Philae mission succeeded on both counts, but Philae's historic landing was marred by its turbulent touchdown. Philae actually landed three different times on Comet 67/P, all because the harpoons designed to secure it in place didn't fire as planned.

After the first landing, Philae bounced up and drifted around the comet for two hours, making another bounce before Rosetta's cameras lost track of it. Scientists figured it was stuck in a shady spot where sunlight couldn't reach its solar panels. Because it was solar-powered, Philae needed to be facing the sun properly to generate enough power for sustained operation on the comet's surface.

Still, Philae did have some power stored in batteries, which lasted for more than two days on the surface. That allowed Philae to perform some science with its 10 instruments in the time it had on Comet 67/P. Most notably, Philae found organic molecules that had never been detected on a comet before.

The Rosetta orbiter continued to orbit Comet 67P until September 2016, and it was in that month -- just weeks before Rosetta itself landed on the comet on Sept. 30, 2016 -- that the spacecraft rediscovered the Philae lander lying on its side in a rocky crevice.

#824. Stronger flu shot linked to nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk

A higher dose of the annual flu vaccine may offer older adults an unexpected benefit: a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease.

In a large study led by researchers at UTHealth Houston, adults ages 65 and older who received a high-dose influenza vaccine were less likely to develop Alzheimer's than those given the standard-dose version. The findings, published in the medical journal Neurology, suggest that the strength of a flu vaccine could matter for more than just protection against influenza.

The discovery grew out of an unexpected conversation between a UTHealth Houston physician and local public health officials. What began as a visit to discuss earlier vaccine research eventually led scientists to investigate whether different flu vaccine doses might be associated with different levels of Alzheimer's risk.

A Surprising Connection Between Flu Vaccines and Alzheimer's

Alzheimer's disease is the leading cause of dementia and an increasingly serious public health concern. In 2025, more than 7 million Americans ages 65 and older were living with the disease, representing approximately 1 in 9 people in that age group. That figure is projected to more than double by 2050.

Researchers have been exploring whether common vaccines might influence the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's. In a 2022 study, a team led by Paul Schulz, MD, found that flu vaccination was associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer's among adults 65 and older.

Schulz is a professor of neurology at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston and director of the Neurocognitive Disorders Center at UTHealth Houston Neurosciences.

Three years after that earlier investigation, Schulz and his colleagues published new research examining a more specific question: Could receiving a stronger flu vaccine be associated with an even greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk?

The idea came from public health officials who had learned about the team's previous findings and invited Schulz to discuss them.

"The public health department had seen our vaccine research and asked if I could come down to talk to them about it," said Schulz, who is the senior author of the study and the Rick McCord Professor in Neurology and Umphrey Family Professor in Neurodegenerative Diseases at McGovern Medical School. "We went through the findings, and they asked if there was a difference with different dosages; I was confused."

Why Older Adults Receive Stronger Flu Shots

As people grow older, their immune systems gradually become less effective at recognizing and fighting infections. This age-related decline can make influenza particularly dangerous for seniors.

To help address that vulnerability, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends high-dose influenza vaccines as a preferred option for adults ages 65 and older. These vaccines contain four times as much influenza antigen as standard-dose shots. Antigens are the components of a vaccine that stimulate the immune system to recognize and defend against a virus.

The higher dose is designed to produce a stronger immune response in older adults, whose immune systems may respond less effectively to conventional vaccines.

Schulz had not previously realized that this stronger formulation was available.

"I was stunned that, as a physician, I didn't know a higher dose was offered," Schulz said.

Annual flu vaccination is recommended broadly, but preventing influenza is especially important for people with Alzheimer's disease. Flu infections and their complications can pose serious health risks for individuals already coping with cognitive impairment.

Before 2022, the CDC did not express a preference for one type of injectable influenza vaccine over another for people ages 65 and older. Instead, the guidance emphasized receiving a flu shot every year, regardless of the specific formulation.

Previous research from UTHealth Houston had already linked inactivated influenza vaccines, which use viruses that cannot cause influenza infection, to a 40% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. However, researchers had not yet determined whether a higher vaccine dose might be associated with additional benefits.

Another practical issue made the question particularly relevant. As the population of older Americans continues to grow, demand for high-dose flu vaccines sometimes exceeds the available supply. Consequently, some seniors receive standard-dose vaccines instead.

This variation gave researchers an opportunity to compare Alzheimer's outcomes among older adults who had received different formulations.

"So we started looking, and sure enough, we were able to put together thousands and thousands of people over the age of 65 who got the high- or low-dose vaccine. They're more at risk for Alzheimer's than anybody else, of course, because it's age-related and we could look at high-dose versus low-dose and see if there was a difference," Schulz said.

Nearly 200,000 Adults Reveal a Significant Difference

To investigate the potential connection, the research team analyzed data from nearly 200,000 men and women ages 65 and older.

The results showed that people who received high-dose influenza vaccines had a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease than those who received the standard-dose formulation.

The researchers reported that standard-dose influenza vaccination was associated with a 40% reduction in Alzheimer's risk, while high-dose vaccination was linked to a reduction of nearly 55%.

The association was particularly pronounced among women, who appeared to experience a greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk with the stronger vaccine.

These findings add to growing evidence of a possible relationship between influenza vaccination and brain health. They also raise important questions about whether the immune response triggered by vaccination might influence biological processes involved in Alzheimer's disease.

However, the findings demonstrate an association rather than establishing cause and effect. Additional research is needed to determine whether high-dose flu vaccination directly reduces the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's and to understand the mechanisms that might explain the connection.

What the Findings Could Mean for Alzheimer's Prevention

With Alzheimer's affecting millions of Americans and the number of cases expected to rise sharply in the coming decades, researchers are searching for practical ways to reduce risk.

The possibility that an existing vaccine could have benefits extending beyond influenza prevention is particularly intriguing. Unlike an entirely new treatment, flu vaccination is already widely used, and higher-dose formulations are specifically designed for older adults.

The new findings suggest that vaccine dosage could be an important consideration in future studies exploring the relationship between the immune system and Alzheimer's disease.

For now, the research provides another reason to investigate the potential benefits of influenza vaccination while emphasizing the need for further studies before drawing conclusions about Alzheimer's prevention.

Avram Samuel Bukhbinder, MD, a graduate of McGovern Medical School who is currently a clinical fellow in neurology at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard University, served as a corresponding author of the study.

Schulz is also a faculty member of The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center UTHealth Houston Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences.

Other contributors from McGovern Medical School included Elizabeth He, visiting scholar in the Department of Neurology; Kristofer Harris, MPH, research coordinator in the Department of Neurology; Mya Rodriguez, graduate research assistant in the Department of Neurology; Kamal Phelps, MD, an alumnus of the Department of Neurology; Jenna Thomas; Gabriela Cruz, MD, resident in the Department of Neurology; and Lauren Jhin.

Researchers from the McWilliams School of Biomedical Informatics at UTHealth Houston also participated. They included Xiaoqian Jiang, PhD, associate vice president for medical AI, chair of the Department of Health Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, and Christopher Sarofim Family Professor in Biomedical Informatics and Bioengineering; Yejin Kim, PhD, assistant professor in the Department of Health Data Science and Artificial Intelligence; Luyao Chen, researcher; and Yaobin Ling, PhD, postdoctoral research fellow.

This supernova imposter erupts every 113 days as the compact object gets close to the unstable massive star.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A cosmic imposter that has faked being a supernova 27 times and counting is actually a hot, luminous, and decidedly unstable star that is being fed on by a vampiric black hole or neutron star, NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory has discovered.

When a massive star reaches the end of the road and runs out of nuclear fuel to power fusion reactions in its core, the star is destroyed in a supernova explosion. That’s what astronomers thought they had found on 11 January 2012, when they observed what appeared to be a supernova on the outskirts of the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, which is about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices.

Yet when the light of the 'supernova' faded, the star was still there, only to continue bursting into light every 113 days.

"For 15 years, astronomers have been watching this star get really bright and then dim again on a regular basis," Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia in Charlottesville said in a statement.

Several other supernova imposters have been observed over the past decade or two. Until now, no one knew what causes these stars to repeatedly cry wolf. Thanks to Chandra’s X-ray vision, Aghakhanloo has led a team of astronomers who think they have now uncovered an explanation.

The supernova imposter is named AT 2016blu, and is a type of star that we call a 'luminous blue variable,' or LBV. These are the most massive and luminous stars in the universe and their extreme characteristics result in them being highly unstable, undergoing intermittent bouts of mass loss as they eject material from their outer layers into the surrounding space.

However, faking a supernova is not part of their typical behavior, so a new way of looking at AT 2016blu was needed.

"To understand the cause of these eruptions, we realized that we needed X-ray data that was timed so that we’d observe the star when it was in an outburst," team member Núria Torres-Albà, also from the University of Virginia in Charlottesville, said.

Aghakhanloo’s team were granted the opportunity to commandeer Chandra to target an outburst of AT 2016blu at the earliest opportunity. That opportunity arose in March 2026.

Chandra had previously and coincidentally looked in the direction of NGC 4559 back in 2001 and 2002 and did not notice anything unusual back then. This time around, however, it captured a powerful blast of X-rays coinciding with yet another false supernova outburst.

The X-ray detection allowed Aghakhanloo’s team to assemble a picture of what is happening. "Until we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldn’t figure out what was making this happen," he said.

Chandra’s X-ray observations indicate that AT 2016blu has an unseen companion, a compact, high-gravity object that is either a neutron star or a stellar-mass black hole on an elliptical 113-day orbit around the luminous blue variable.

Neutron stars and stellar-mass black holes are the core remnants of massive stars that have gone supernova for real, meaning that at one time AT 2016blu was a binary star system.

Each time the compact object reaches the point in its orbit that is closest to the luminous blue variable, its powerful gravity is able to pull material from the unstable star. This sets in motion a chain of events that results in the brilliant outbursts.

As the stolen starstuff is dragged away from the wounded star and towards the compact object, it forms an accretion disk swirling around the neutron star or black hole so fast and growing so hot that it emits X-rays. These are the X-rays that Chandra saw.

The X-rays are immense, energizing the surrounding cloud of material that had been ejected by the luminous blue variable years before. The cloud is heated and glows extremely brightly in visible light, creating the impression of a supernova.

"We suspected that the bright repeating flashes at optical wavelengths might actually be powered by periodic blasts of high-energy X-rays," said team member Nathan Smith of the University of Arizona in Tucson. "The dense gas surrounding the system is heated by the X-rays and then glows in the optical."

Calculations suggest that each year a 440 billion trillion pounds of material at minimum is stolen by the compact object, and possibly two orders of magnitude more than that. This is a huge amount, yet it is only 800 millionths of the mass of the sun, and AT 2016blu’s luminous blue variable is at least 33 times the mass of the sun.

Nevertheless, it is far greater than the maximum rate of material that a neutron star can safely accrete, referred to as the Eddington limit. It’s little wonder that the accretion onto the compact object unleashes such extreme energies.

AT 2016blu is also connected with another mysterious and rare astrophysical phenomenon, that of ultra-luminous X-ray (ULX) sources. The identity of whatever it is that is powering ULXs remains unclear, but the involvement of compact objects such as black holes and neutron stars is high on the list.

AT 2016blu is bright enough to be considered a ULX, so could it act as a Rosetta stone connecting supernova imposters with ULXs? It’s too early to say that; only one other supernova impostor has so far been found to have X-ray emission typical of material being stolen from one star and accreting onto a compact body, and that is SN 2010da, but in that case it is known that the companion is another massive star, a red supergiant, rather than a compact object.

The X-ray detection of AT 2016blu is described in a paper published on Monday (Nov. 9) in The Astrophysical Journal.

He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

#819. Burnham urges caution on scrapping 3pm TV blackout

The blackout originated in the 1960s when Burnley chairman Bob Lord encouraged the EFL to oppose television coverage of 15:00 Saturday matches

Andy Burnham has urged caution on lifting the Saturday 3pm TV blackout in the UK, saying the health of the football pyramid should come first.

The rule was introduced in the 1960s to encourage fans to attend lower league games and prevents matches from being shown on UK television between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on Saturdays.

The blackout, which is enforced by Article 48 of the Uefa Statutes and is imposed by the English and Scottish football associations, comes into effect when 50% of fixtures in the top two divisions are scheduled to kick off at 3pm.

The Premier League is in the middle of a record Â£6.7bn domestic TV deal for Sky and TNT to show up to 270 live games a season.

But there could be room for change with the 3pm rule in the upcoming broadcast cycle, as the rights deals for the Premier League, EFL and SPFL all end in 2028-29.

The prime minister said any decision to remove the ban would require careful thought about the consequences.

"I would urge a bit of caution [on the blackout], because it does protect the income of lower-league clubs," Burnham said.

Scottish football could pave way for 3pm TV blackout to end

Why does football have Saturday 3pm TV blackout in UK?

"If you have effectively wall-to-wall Premier League football at any time, it takes away perhaps the incentive to go and watch the football league or non-league.

"So I think it has to be considered carefully. I'm not going to take the pure consumer view here. I'll take the health-of-football approach to this particular issue."

Only the FA Cup final, which traditionally kicks off at 3pm, is allowed to be broadcast during the blackout window.

In October, the SPFL said it is "flexible about the number of games" that will form part of the TV new deal, which BBC Sport understands includes matches shown on a Saturday afternoon.

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters has previously said a decision about whether the blackout stays in place would need to be made in the future.

But Burnham added: "I would first of all want to protect the football pyramid before I agree to saying 'let's have even more live football'".

"I think it's about protecting the experience with the paying supporter, protecting the football pyramid. Those issues matter to me, first of all."

#818. Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease

Tick-borne illnesses are becoming increasingly common across the United States, and Lyme disease remains the most frequently reported. Nearly 500,000 Americans are diagnosed each year. The infection is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, which typically reaches humans through the bite of an infected blacklegged tick. Antibiotics can treat Lyme disease, but without treatment, the infection may affect the joints, heart, and nervous system. Some patients also experience symptoms that persist over time.

Now, one of the longest-running studies of Lyme disease ecology is challenging several assumptions about what makes the disease more likely to spread. For more than 35 years, scientists at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in Millbrook, New York, have tracked the complicated relationships among ticks, mice, oak trees, predators, and weather. Their research has uncovered unexpected patterns that could help predict when people face greater exposure to infected ticks.

A new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences brings together nine of the project's most surprising discoveries. The findings show how decades of observations can reveal connections that shorter studies might miss.

"On balance, these surprises have enriched our knowledge of this system, helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk," said lead author Richard Ostfeld, a disease ecologist at the Cary Institute who leads the research program alongside Shannon LaDeau.

According to Ostfeld, the extensive data collected over the years have been essential for separating meaningful ecological patterns from coincidences and statistical fluctuations.

"Studies of this depth and length are incredibly rare," said LaDeau. "This research has followed an ecological community -- including oak trees, mammals, and microorganisms -- examining how interactions like predation, parasitism, and competition shape the system over time. The evolution of understanding summarized in this paper is something you simply cannot get without such a long-term and system-focused study."

Deer May Play a Smaller Role in Lyme Disease Risk Than Expected

When Lyme disease first gained recognition in the United States during the 1980s, white-tailed deer were considered a likely driver of rising tick populations. Hunters frequently encountered deer carrying numerous adult ticks, suggesting that areas with more deer might also produce more ticks.

The reasoning seemed straightforward. Although deer cannot pass the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks, they provide blood meals for adult female ticks. Scientists suspected that larger deer populations would allow more female ticks to reproduce, eventually increasing the number of young ticks capable of spreading the infection.

But decades of monitoring have produced a different picture. On the Cary Institute's 2,000-acre forested research property in Dutchess County, New York, researchers found no statistically significant connection between deer numbers and the abundance of nymphal ticks. Nymphs are immature ticks responsible for much of the Lyme disease transmission to humans.

"We had detected a weak positive relationship between deer and subsequent nymph abundance over short subsets of the data," said Ostfeld, "but the whole data set in its entirety shows no such thing."

Mice Are a Much Stronger Predictor of Tick Surges

While deer populations failed to predict the abundance of nymphal ticks, mouse populations showed a much clearer relationship.

Years with especially large mouse populations were followed by approximately 40% more nymphal ticks the next year. White-footed mice are particularly important because they provide excellent blood meals for tick larvae and are highly effective at transmitting Borrelia burgdorferi to those feeding on them.

Once infected as larvae, ticks can retain the bacteria as they develop into nymphs. When these nymphs take another blood meal, they can pass the infection to humans.

The findings suggest that tracking mouse populations could provide a valuable early warning of unusually high tick numbers.

How Acorns Can Predict Tick Populations Two Years Ahead

One of the most unexpected discoveries involves something that might seem entirely unrelated to Lyme disease: acorns.

Oak trees periodically produce exceptionally large crops of acorns in synchronized events known as acorn masting. These unusually productive years provide an abundance of food for forest rodents, allowing mouse populations to expand during the following year.

That increase in mice then supports larger numbers of young ticks. As a result, the researchers found that a particularly heavy acorn crop can reliably predict an increase in nymphal ticks two years later.

The relationship reveals a remarkable sequence of events in which the reproductive cycle of forest trees helps determine future tick abundance. It also offers researchers another potential tool for anticipating periods of greater Lyme disease exposure.

Why More Mice Don't Always Mean More Infected Ticks

Although mouse abundance helps predict how many nymphal ticks will appear, the researchers discovered that it does not consistently predict what percentage of those ticks will carry Lyme disease bacteria.

Initially, scientists expected both measures to rise together. Because mice are efficient transmitters of B. burgdorferi, an increase in mice seemed likely to produce not only more ticks but also a greater proportion of infected ticks.

Early observations appeared to support that idea. However, as additional years of data accumulated, the apparent relationship gradually disappeared.

"It kept me up at night," said Ostfeld, "because it meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong."

The explanation appears to involve the other animals that share the forest with mice. Skunks, squirrels, and opossums also serve as hosts for feeding ticks, but most are much less effective at passing the Lyme disease bacterium to them.

When these animals are abundant, more larval ticks may feed on hosts that are unlikely to infect them. This can reduce the percentage of nymphal ticks carrying the bacteria, even when mouse populations are high.

"So the infection prevalence in the nymphs really depends on how all the larval tick meals are distributed across all the hosts," explained Ostfeld. "It would have been convenient if one host predicted that for us, but that has not been the case."

This finding highlights an important distinction between the total number of ticks in an environment and the proportion carrying the pathogen. Predicting the risk of infection requires understanding the broader community of animals that ticks feed on, not simply counting mice.

Extreme Heat and Cold May Not Kill Ticks in the Wild

Weather has also produced some unexpected results.

Earlier laboratory experiments suggested that exposure to intense heat or severe cold could kill blacklegged ticks. Yet observations in natural habitats revealed that ticks are surprisingly capable of surviving these conditions.

Researchers believe ticks protect themselves from temperature extremes by retreating into deeper soil layers or hiding beneath fallen leaves, where conditions are less severe than at the surface.

However, the long-term data also revealed a more complicated relationship with temperature. Years that are warmer overall tend to be followed by fewer nymphal ticks than usual, despite the ability of individual ticks to withstand short periods of extreme heat.

At the same time, warmer conditions generally favor mouse populations, which can lead to more ticks. These opposing effects make it difficult to predict how changing temperatures will ultimately influence Lyme disease risk.

What 35 Years of Research Mean for Lyme Disease Prevention

Taken together, the discoveries show that Lyme disease risk depends on a network of ecological interactions that is complicated but not entirely unpredictable.

Mouse abundance, for example, provides a stronger indicator of future nymphal tick numbers than deer abundance at the study site. Similarly, unusually harsh winters may not reduce tick populations as dramatically as previously expected.

By understanding these patterns, public health officials may be better equipped to anticipate periods of increased tick exposure and develop more effective prevention strategies.

Still, important questions remain, particularly about how climate change will affect ticks, the animals they feed on, and the oak trees that influence rodent populations.

"You would expect that a warming climate, which makes life better for the mice, would eventually make life better for the ticks, but we have not seen that so far," said Ostfeld. "We need to know what to expect from the different manifestations of climate change, which are sometimes warmer and drier, and sometimes warmer and wetter. The time of year when it's very warm also matters to ticks, oaks, and acorn production."

The research site in Dutchess County has undergone significant environmental changes since monitoring began in 1991. Climate shifts, changes to the surrounding landscape, and the arrival of invasive species have all altered the conditions in which the forest's plants and animals live.

Researchers intend to continue following these changes to determine how ticks and their hosts respond over time. Their work could provide increasingly valuable insights into how future environmental changes will influence human exposure to Lyme disease and other infections carried by ticks.

Materials provided by Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#817. Klopp says Infantino worse than Blatter

Jurgen Klopp took over as Germany head coach in July

Germany head coach Jurgen Klopp says he "didn't think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that" as he called for Fifa president Gianni Infantino to be replaced.

Blatter resigned as Fifa boss in 2015 amid a corruption scandal and was succeeded by Infantino in February 2016.

Infantino plans to stand for re-election in March but has been under pressure since scrapping his Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, which included selling off stakes in the World Cup and other Fifa competitions to private investors.

Infantino apologised to the Fifa Council for the plan but was told he was not fit to lead world football's governing body unless he released all the documents and answered key questions.

"I've been following football for many years. There are people who are much more knowledgeable about this than I am. But I think most people now agree a change would make a lot of sense," said former Liverpool boss Klopp.

"I didn't think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that."

Klopp added: "Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job."

French Football Federation (FFF) president Philippe Diallo has been named as Uefa's candidate to challenge Infantino.

Diallo received the unanimous support of Uefa's executive committee and formal ratification from the FFF is expected on Tuesday.

Uefa, which is European football's governing body, said it has "full confidence" Diallo would "uphold the highest standards of governance" amid its calls for "renewed unity and trust within the global football community".

Wenger decides not to challenge Fifa chief Infantino

Infantino apologises to Fifa Council - but told he is still not fit to lead

Uefa has been one of Infantino's fiercest critics and has repeatedly called on him to stand down.

It has prepared criminal legal proceedings against Infantino and lodged a claim in three US courts for all documents related to FFE to be released.

The deadline for candidates to officially confirm they are standing against Infantino in Fifa's presidential election is Wednesday.

Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger, who is Fifa's head of global development, had been considering running for the job but sources have told BBC Sport he has ruled himself out.

Former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega was the first person to put his name forward in October.

Japan Football Association honorary president Kozo Tashima has also announced his intention to stand.

"There are people who truly care about the future of football - people who aren't driven by financial interests," said Klopp.

"If someone like that were to step up - if someone like that were to become president - I think that would be a significant improvement.

"There are surely people who care deeply about the future of football and have no financial interests in it."
