#746. ‘The Traitors’ Star Ben McDonnell on ‘New Blood’ Set Secrets and Alan Cumming: “You Can Never Break Character”

The gay cowboy from the first-ever all-civilian season that aired on NBC shares his own secrets — like being an actor and never breaking character — and what it's really like to film on the Emmy-winning Scottish castle set.

[The following story contains spoilers through the 10th episode of The Traitors: New Blood.]

Ben McDonnell had just finished bingeing every episode of The Traitors when he got the call to join the fifth season of the Peacock and NBC Emmy-winning reality competition. The barrel racer living on a ranch in Texas with his husband, where he hosts his weekly comedy podcast It’s Ben a Week, accepted the gig, which he considers one of his biggest challenges yet, and quickly found himself heading to the Scottish castle to live with strangers and host Alan Cumming. McDonnell became the King of One Liners and the fan- and cast-favorite gay cowboy — until his elimination in the penultimate episode that aired last week. Related Stories TV Jason Benetti Will Replace Dan Hicks on Notre Dame Play-by-Play Saturday Following Sudden Passing (Exclusive) 'Dancing' Diaries After 'DWTS' Season 35, Mark Ballas Would Love His Wife BC Jean to Be His Next Celebrity Partner

“Every morning I would wake up freaking out [about getting eliminated]. And for some reason, the day I got murdered, I was so calm,” McDonnell says when speaking to The Hollywood Reporter after his exit. McDonnell went onto the show assuming his personality would make him a Traitor, but being a Faithful sent him away from the series with something more valuable than the $250,000 prize money. “I didn’t think they were going to love me for me,” he says of his castmates. “And that part was healing in an unexpected way, when you didn’t even know you were broken to be healed.”

Below, when opening up to THR, McDonnell reveals a surprise for fans and his castmates (he’s actually a trained actor), talks about the hardest parts about filming, like giving up his phone (“People are going to think I’m going to rehab,” he remembers thinking) and why Cumming is a national treasure who inspired the name of McDonnell’s new piglet, Alan Cunningham.

As a trained actor who left L.A. for a Texas ranch, how did Hollywood pull you back for this show?

This experience was truly one of the most exciting acting experiences of my life. When you’re on a set, you show up to play a character, but then when the director says “cut,” you go back to being Ben. When you’re playing Traitors, the director never says cut. You are in character at all times. Even when the cameras are not rolling, you still have to play whatever character you’re showing up as. If you’re having lunch, you can never break character. You have to play it up the whole time.

I have a pretty large and loud personality, so I really had to tone it back, which was challenging because I want to be the center of attention. I wanna go be loud, but that’s immediately going to put a target on my back. I also didn’t tell anyone that I was an actor. I really leaned in to, “I’m this gay cowboy,” which is not a lie. I really am the gay cowboy. It’s just that the gay cowboy is more of a hobby than my career.

The producers hired me to play a game about lying and deceit. But the show is non-union, so there are definitely people there who aren’t trying to pursue an acting or Hollywood career. For instance, Abby L. didn’t even have Instagram before she got on the show. She’s an astrophysicist, so she must be a fan of the show and then applied. There are people from all different walks of life, which was amazing.

I went to BravoCon and saw this Traitors thing, and I remember asking my friend, “What is Traitors?” She was like, “You don’t watch Traitors?” I had never seen it. She’s like, “You have to watch. It’s the best show.” I was like, whatever. Then in Texas, we got an insane ice storm last January and here in Texas, when you get an ice storm, you’re stuck at home because no one knows how to drive.

AJ, my husband, came out one day like, “What are you watching?” I’m like, “Let’s just watch this Traitors thing.” I turn on one episode — instantly hooked. I binged every season of the U.K. show, every season of the U.S. show. Then two weeks later I got the phone call: “Would you be interested in The Traitors?” I was like, “I just binged it. This is crazy.”

Next thing you know, I’m at a Scottish castle with Alan Cumming, playing Clue, basically, in the middle of the Scottish Highlands.

Were you pursuing acting at the time? Or do you feel like it was lucky timing?

Acting has always been my main goal. As an actor, I never thought I would do reality TV. For a long time, I was opposed. I’ve had other offers in life for a reality show idea, and I’ve always been like, “You can’t do reality and be taken seriously as an actor.” I do feel there has been a shift. Like, 10 years ago when I was like, “I can’t be gay and be an actor because I’m going to be put in this box where you’re just the gay actor.” That is totally not the case anymore. You can be gay and play straight roles, you can be straight and play gay roles. It’s not as scary as it used to be.

So same thing with reality. You you look at people like our Ariana Madix from Vanderpump Rules. She’s on Broadway. She’s on an NBC show. She’s doing all sorts of stuff. There are so many different reality stars who are now pursuing scripted. So I guess it was not quite as scary, but scripted television and movies have always been number one.

I know you were hoping to be a Traitor. What was your strategy going in? And did your strategy change once you found out you were a Faithful?

I had only thought about being a Traitor. It was so set in my mind.. There was absolutely no question of me not being a Traitor. Stupidly, that did not even enter my brain. Preparing for the show, flying over there in the castle. At no point was I like, “What am I going to do if I’m a Faithful?”

So when I didn’t feel the tap on my shoulder, I remember being like, “Do I need to ask someone if didn’t feel the tap? Like, for sure, I’m a Traitor.” And when I was a Faithful, I laid in bed that night and was like, “Well, now what?”

If you’re a Traitor, it’s strategy all the way. You need to plan. You need to think 10 steps ahead. If you’re a Faithful, it’s a popularity contest. We are back in high school, and you need the Traitors to think you trust them so they want to keep you around, and you need the Faithful to like you so that they don’t banish you. You can watch every season of every Traitors in every different country. What you think would work with one group of people may not work with the next. You have no idea how different people will react.

Personally, I think my training at The Groundlings and with improv really helped me roll with the punches. You had to go with it. I really didn’t try to overthink it. Once I was a Faithful, I’m like, “Just be honest.” And it got me quite far.

This is a huge thing to keep secret from family, friends, work. What was that like for you? Did you tell anyone?

AJ is the only person I told. When you go to Scotland to film, you have no phone. No internet. No connection to the outside world. I was gone during my birthday. It’s very overwhelming.

I actually thought I was going to miss not having my phone. It was so nice and relaxing to not have a phone. The only thing that would drive me nuts is wondering, “Who’s trying to contact me?” I was like, “People are going to think I’m going to rehab.” (Laughs.)

I’m very active on social media. I post on my story all the time. The fact that I’ve just gone completely quiet? Also, I had to record my podcast, It’s Ben a Week, in advance. I had to get all the social media clips. So my podcast Instagram posted a clip every single day. But I was like, “What if I’m causing drama and I’m not even responding?” You have no control.

Let’s go inside your elimination. You were very calm. What did you mean when you said, “I knew it was time” before you opened the envelope and found out you were murdered?

I’m one of the calmest people I know. Nothing riles me up that much. I’m always like, “It’s fine.” That’s my line. This show caused so much anxiety! I’ve never had anxiety. I’m like, “Can someone get me a Xanax, please? (Laughs.) Because I think I need one.”

So every morning I would wake up freaking out. And for some reason, the day I got murdered, I was so calm. That morning I actually started packing my things. I knew there was something coming. That fur coat that I wore? I brought that to wear either at the finale or when I’m murdered. I even talked about with the stylist about saving that coat, and that day, I brought the coat with me.

When I opened the door, I saw the envelope and there was a little hint of me that was like, “Maybe I’m being recruited [to be a Traitor,]” which I was like, “What a dream.” And then I was like, I don’t think so. That’s when I was like, it was time. I was ready to go.

What’s the exit process like? Do you leave right after that?

You do more confessionals. You’re there for a whole other day doing stuff. But you don’t get to say goodbye to anyone. Shooting the show is such an immersive experience that you have to remind yourself no one is dying. They don’t waste money on budget or any of the production value. That funeral scene, for example, when we were in the graveyard and there was smoke and fog and you see a gravestone with your name on it? You’re watching your friends get into coffins in the ground. It feels real. Then the exits are abrupt; no goodbyes. It’s like, boom, gone.

Did you make it further than you thought, or did you think you could win?

I definitely made it farther than I thought. Every day, when I’d walk into breakfast, I’d do a sigh of relief. There are so many steps to get there, I did not want to be the first one eliminated. Then we’re halfway through it, and by the time you can see the end of the tunnel. It’s like, “Let’s just finish it.”

But if I’m being really honest, after the feast and hearing some of the other people’s stories, like Abby B and Shane and some of the other contestants opening up, I was like, “I actually think there are other people who deserve the money more than me.” I truly feel like if I would have won the money, I may have had guilt.

I would love to have an extra $250,000. But I think there are other people where it can change their life.

Are you still going to “haunt” Katie, or are you over it?

No, I’m still haunting her. (Laughs.) She’s great, and I don’t blame her. Obviously, it’s part of the game. But I was onto her for a while.

You opened up about yourself — what it was like growing up gay in Wisconsin and parts about your family life. What about this process lends you to open up in the way that you did?

I’m not a very emotional person. Not many people have ever seen me cry. Everything I do in life is with humor, whether that’s deflecting pain or hurt. So, those emotions you saw were very real and raw. Growing up as a gay kid in a small town in Wisconsin, being bullied in school for being gay, and then having a super traumatic experience with my stepdad. He literally held a gun to my head when he found out I was gay.

I’ve kind of struggled with male relationships. I’m much more comfortable with women, and then with gay men, it’s like, “Is this friendship? Does someone want more here?” I do have male friends. I wanted to clear that up. But I would say 99 percent of my friends are female. So going into the castle, I had zero expectation of making any friends. I’m like, “I’m just here to play this game; get in, get out.” And I made such good friends with so many people on the cast.

In my interviews leading up to it, I had said, “I’m going to be the girl’s gay best friend. I’m the social butterfly. And the guys will see me as an asset because I am a 6-foot-3 Sasquatch that lives on a ranch. I can do all these challenges. They’re going to love me for that.” But I didn’t think they were going to love me for me. And that part was healing in an unexpected way, when you didn’t even know you were broken to be healed.

In that moment, I said I feel like I’ve already won, which I also think is another reason why I was so at peace leaving. I had a great experience. I had so much fun. I got to come play Clue with all these fun people in the Scottish Highlands and Alan Cumming, a national treasure. It checked every box for me.

From a filming standpoint, behind the scenes, going from viewer to being a part of it. What is something we don’t realize about the show, the filming schedule, about Alan?

You could watch TV. You get Netflix, Hulu, Amazon, Disney. I was trying so hard to get cocktails in the castle. You’re only allowed a certain amount of alcoholic drinks, and I just wanted a drink to take the edge off. I always drink a Whitney Houston, which is a vodka and Diet Coke. They would give you a drink made and then one time, they brought it to me, and the shot was tiny. I switched to red wine. I would take the wine, and pour it into my coffee cups, and I was hiding it in the closet. Then when you had a day off, I would drink the wine hiding in the closet. (Laughs.)

But I think the thing people would be surprised to know is that Alan sits in those round tables the whole time. They are really long. You see five minutes. They’re sometimes two hours long. He sits there the entire time, and he never breaks character.

The one time we got a glimpse of him breaking character is when he told me he wanted a pig. And that’s when I go, “Pigs are the new dogs.” We actually have a brand new piglet we just got, and his name is Alan. I sent him pictures and he said, “Oh my God, did you name that pig after me?” I go, “Of course. His name is Alan Cunningham.” He was dying.

Also as an actor to watch him? He’s an icon. I would love to be an actor like Alan Cumming, where you can do so many different things and play so many different characters and have such a long career. What an inspiration. It was almost like I was doing a movie with Alan Cumming.

What’s something about the format you’d change?

I would make it longer because I really think this cast of people was so interesting and dynamic. People came from all different backgrounds. I really don’t think you got to see how cool and special everyone was and is, and the relationships. Tamika and I were ride-or-die besties from day one, and no one even knew we were friends. You don’t see any of it. So I wish people got to see more — and maybe a little more airtime for Ben!

Is there something about you that you want people to know that we didn’t get to see?

A lot of my friends, or people who know me, said, “You are so quiet and calm, and flying under the radar,” and that is so not who I am. I’m loud, energetic. Usually people would say I’m life of the party. So I’m definitely much larger than life than I was shown on the show. But I also think you got to see a more sensitive, nice side of me on the show.

You’ve been called King of the One Liners. Which one are you most proud of?

“Shut up, Jay” was an iconic line. I think “pigs are the new dog,” and also comparing that Victor and Cher will live forever.

Is there anything you want to say in response to things you’ve read from your castmates who’ve been doing interviews?

(Laughs.) There are some castmates out there who have had some strong opinions. I think that in the climate we live in, gay people have had it hard enough. I don’t understand why another gay guy is out there trying to bash people or tear people down. We really should be building each other up. I don’t see the point in that.

How do you feel about reality shows now? Would you do another one?

Scripted will always be my front and center, and the ultimate goal. But I’ve never been one to say no. So I’m not closing any doors. I think I could do a little Dancing With the Stars.

You have your podcast, It’s Ben a Week, which is the most appropriate title for this moment. It’s a weekly comedy, pop culture show. Will you have Traitors stars on, now that you can finally talk about the show?

Yes, now that I’m able to. That was really hard for me. It’s Ben a Week really has been my baby for years. I’m a one-man band. I book my own guests, edit my own shows. I do all my own social media. I spoke about this on a recent episode: It’s been really hard to not to talk about it. It’s almost like I couldn’t be honest these last few months. Traitors has taken over my entire world, and I wasn’t able to talk about it. Every week I’m coming on talking about how it’s been a week, but I can’t really talk about what my week has been. I’m excited that now I can speak on it and share my experience.

I’m opening the invitation to any of the castmembers who want to come on. I know a lot of them will because we’re good friends, but the invitation is open to all of the castmembers. I also have some other cast from previous seasons who will be coming on , so you’re going to hear from some other Faithfuls and Traitors.

I love comedy podcasts and casual conversations, which is something I try to do. I want to sit in my car and feel like we’re all hanging out together. I want people to feel like they’re hanging out with their friend Ben. I love Las Culturistas with Matt Rogers and Bowen Yang. I love Long Winded with Gabby Windey. She’s been on The Traitors. The fact that she can just sit by herself and talk for an hour and how she rambles and how smart she is and quick witted, I love her. It’s the funniest thing. I also listen to, Sorry, We’re Cyrus, which is Brandi and Tish Cyrus. I listen to Chelsea Handler. And, of course, I listen to Call Her Daddy because she gets some really, really cool guests.

What’s your dream acting role? I hear Taylor Sheridan lives in your neighborhood.

Taylor lives right down the street. He’s filming so many shows. I’m pretty sure he has a new partnership with NBC that’s starting up the next couple years. … I can literally ride my horse to set. Taylor, you have an actor in your backyard who has his own horses he can ride to set. I don’t even need a stunt double!

I love comedies like Schitt’s Creek. A David in Schitt’s Creek. I love Grace and Frankie. I would love one of those shows that has a cultlike following. I think everyone wants that!

Half of me loves the comedy, but then I can put that cowboy hat on. I just did a movie that comes out next year, called Cowboy. It’s a gay cowboy movie where I play the straight cowboy. On Traitors, I’ve been portrayed as this gay cowboy, but I also can play the straight cowboy.

The next batch of Traitors will be back to celebrities. Any advice for them now that you’ve been through it?

Celebrities have it so much harder, because everyone knows everyone. I’m a Real Housewives fan, so when I’m watching The Traitors, I’m always rooting for the Housewives. But even if you don’t watch Housewives, you know Lisa Rinna’s reputation. She can’t go on the show and try to lie or be something else. I had the opportunity where I could change my personality a little bit or be what I wanted everyone to believe.

But I guess, try to be yourself and try to make friends.

What about your season — who are you rooting for to win on Thursday? Where are you watching the finale?

I’ll be watching the finale in New York at Club Cumming, Alan’s club. I have my alliance with Clyde and Abby B, so I really would hope for them to win. And of course, my sweaty boy, Victor. I’m excited to see the finale and who is going to win, or what group. Faithful or Traitor?

I tried, and they were like, “That’s a hard no.” (Laughs.) I did get to take some of the wardrobe. You bring your own wardrobe, but if you wear some of their stuff, you get to keep it. I did get some really cool pants!

The two-part Traitors finale releases Thursday at 8 p.m. on Peacock; all episodes stream on Peacock.

#744. James Bond Fans Already Complaining About Robert Pattinson: “Not Alpha Male”

As is the ritual, the new Bond choice is getting gripes from franchise fans: "I've seen sexier potatoes."

There are many great reasons for casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond.

But in the wake of Amazon-MGM Studios announcing the Batman actor as the seventh 007, plenty of fans are griping online about the choice.

Such complaints are to be expected, of course. Any actor cast as Bond is going to get bashed. Even Daniel Craig was roundly criticized by fans when producers tapped the character actor as Bond back in 2005 (“he isn’t handsome enough,” “Bond can’t be blonde,” etc.) Our visual concept of Bond is entirely formed by the other six actors who have played the role, so anybody new is going to be tough to imagine — at least, at first. Related Stories Movies James Bond Found: Robert Pattinson to Play 007 Movies Matt Damon Reveals Ben Affleck's Review of 'The Odyssey' -- and the One Performance He Couldn't Stop Talking About

That said, the Pattinson complaints are interesting, perhaps even valuable, as they show producers what they’re up against in terms of preconceived notions about their casting choice.

The comment section of the British tabloid Daily Mail has been a hive of Pattinson bashing all morning.

Wrote one: “He lacks the magnetic charm, polished elegance, rugged confidence, seductive sophistication, and effortless swagger that define James Bond.” Similarly penned another: “He doesn’t stand out as having the animal masculinity or charisma of a Bond character.” Another opined: “He doesn’t come across as Alpha male, ladies man, action type.” Snarked another: “I’ve seen sexier potatoes.”

Others felt that Pattinson has had too many iconic roles and expressed frustration that the same actors seem to be cast in so many projects.

“You can’t have the same actor playing Batman and James Bond at the same time,” wrote one. “The Broccoli family would have never made this decision.” Or as one fan elaborated on Amazon MGM Studios’ Instagram post: “If you want to make a James Bond truly immortal, you have to cast someone who isn’t already strongly associated with other iconic movie characters.”

Or wrote one Redditor: “I’m not fond of this choice. I’d much rather see him continue his very interesting career as he has been excellent in so many roles & then have a newly discovered talent or up & comer to play Bond.”

One influencer on X called the casting a “disappointingly unimaginative choice … Do we really have such a shortage of actors that we need the same handful of guys playing every iconic character? … This feels like a lazy, risk-averse pick designed to hedge Amazon’s bets by casting an established star.”

A recurring comment is that Pattinson would have been better as the next film’s villain, though this probably has some recency bias coming off his heel turn in The Odyssey and his creepy take on Chris Hanson in Primetime. “He doesn’t feel like Bond. He’d have a made a fantastic Bond villain though,” one fan wrote on Reddit. But as another countered: “The fact people say he would make a good Bond villain is one of the main reasons I’m excited for him to instead be Bond.”

Of course, plenty (if not most) reactions online have been positive, and even some of his detractors begrudgingly admit that Pattinson is a terrific actor who will probably crush the role.

The truth is there’s too much at stake — and too many talented people behind the scenes in a Bond production — for any actor cast in the role to outright fail. Any of the actors who were under consideration could have been made to work, and Pattinson, one suspects, will have less of a hill to climb than others given his star power and franchise experience. A week or two after the opening of Bond 26, Pattinson will have evolved from a decision made by producers and a studio to simply being Bond (James Bond).

#743. NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovers a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields

Turbulence is all around us, from milk swirling into a cup of coffee to powerful storms churning through the atmosphere and oceans. But turbulence also occurs throughout space, where it behaves in ways that scientists are still struggling to understand.

Unlike the air and water on Earth, much of the matter in space consists of electrically charged particles in a state (known as the plasma state). These particles interact strongly with magnetic and electric fields, creating turbulence that is fundamentally different from what we experience on Earth. Space plasma is also so thinly spread that particles rarely collide with one another, making its behavior even more unusual.

Scientists have long struggled to explain how turbulence develops under these conditions and how energy is distributed among its constantly changing fluctuations. Now, an international research team has uncovered a surprising clue: hidden within the seemingly random motion of space plasma is a distinct magnetic pattern that reverses direction at very small scales.

The discovery, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, reveals a previously unobserved phenomenon that could improve our understanding of the solar wind and the turbulent conditions that influence space weather.

NASA's Parker Solar Probe Reveals a Hidden Magnetic Reversal

Researchers from the Technische Universität Braunschweig and the University of Tokyo, working with Tohoku University, Kyushu University, Osaka University, and other international institutions, identified the phenomenon using observations from NASA's Parker Solar Probe.

The collaboration brought together scientists from ten countries, including researchers at the Institute of Theoretical Physics at Technische Universität Braunschweig.

By analyzing highly precise measurements of magnetic fields and particles, the team discovered that turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation at a particular range of wavelengths. This marks the first direct observation of such a reversal in space turbulence.

Even more surprisingly, the reversal becomes more pronounced and shifts toward longer wavelengths as the solar wind travels farther from the Sun.

The change occurs at a critical boundary where the behavior of plasma shifts from the collective movement of a flowing fluid to the dynamics of individual particles. This connection suggests that the magnetic reversal may provide an important new way to understand how turbulence operates across different physical scales.

Finding Order in the Chaos of Space Turbulence

At larger scales, plasma moves much like a fluid. Swirling structures called vortices and electromagnetic waves create increasingly complex fluctuations, producing the turbulent conditions found throughout space.

Although these movements appear random, the researchers discovered that the rotation of the magnetic fields follows a consistent pattern.

When viewed along a direction pointing outward from the Sun, magnetic fields at larger scales tend to rotate counterclockwise. At much smaller scales, however, the preferred rotation switches to clockwise.

This reversal occurs precisely where plasma stops behaving primarily like a fluid and begins exhibiting behavior governed by individual particles.

The finding is particularly striking because it reveals a clear, organized feature within a system otherwise dominated by seemingly unpredictable fluctuations.

"We see a clear structure in the spectrum, even though the turbulence represents unstructured motions," says Dr. Masatomi Iizawa (TU Braunschweig), the study's first author.

Dr. Yokoi (University. of Tokyo) emphasizes the broader importance of the discovery, stating, "The results are of great significance for both plasma physics and astrophysics."

Why the Discovery Matters for Solar Storms and Space Weather

Although the magnetic reversal occurs at extremely small scales, understanding it could have far-reaching consequences for space physics.

Plasma turbulence is a major feature of many environments throughout the universe, including Earth's magnetosphere, the solar wind, regions affected by solar eruptions, interplanetary space, and the disks of material surrounding astronomical objects known as accretion disks.

It also influences the shock waves and clouds of magnetic material that travel through interplanetary space following eruptions on the Sun.

These disturbances can play an important role in geomagnetic storms, making plasma turbulence a critical factor in efforts to predict space weather.

By showing how an organized magnetic pattern emerges as turbulent plasma transitions from fluid behavior to particle behavior, the new research provides an important piece of a longstanding physics puzzle. The findings could ultimately help scientists better understand the complex processes that govern the solar wind and improve the physical models used to forecast geomagnetic storms.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029.

Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky.

It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth.

The spectacular display occurs just once every 2-2.5 years, when Mars catches up to Jupiter as it plies its more distant orbit, making the pair appear side by side from our Earthly vantage point — an event known to astronomers as an appulse.

Both Mars and Jupiter are "superior planets" whose orbits exist beyond that of Earth. As a result their disks always appear full to us through the eyepiece of a telescope, unlike the inner planets Mercury and Venus, which exhibit moon-like phases as they circle the sun.

A 6-inch telescope can reveal the wildly differing natures of the solar system worlds. Slew your scope to Jupiter to spot the gargantuan cloud bands (and zones) that ring the gas giant, formed from masses of ammonia and water that travel in different directions through Jupiter's hydrogen and helium atmosphere, driven by powerful jet streams.

Mars, meanwhile, appears as a reddish, ochre disk complete with dark surface features, where basaltic rock has been scoured clean of the iron-rich dust that covers much of its surface, according to NASA.

Interested in seeing and capturing the planets for yourself? Then be sure to read our guide on everything you need to observe and photograph the planets of the solar system, along with our picks of the top telescopes, cameras and lenses for exploring the night sky in 2026.

#741. Architecture of a portal complex embedded in the poxvirus core

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Gene transcription within the viral core is a distinctive feature of poxvirus replication. Following entry into the cytoplasm, the poxvirus core dissociates from the lateral bodies and undergoes expansion, functioning as a compartment for early transcription1. However, how molecules are exchanged between the viral core and the host cytoplasm remains poorly understood. Here, using cryo-electron tomography and sub-tomogram averaging, we determine the structures of the portal complex and its central pore on the vaccinia virus core at 6.7 Å and 4.4 Å resolution, respectively. Guided by structural predictions and experimental density, we identify three viral proteins, E8, E6 and L3, as the principal components of the pore and construct a structural model of their organization. The pore contains a narrow, positively charged constriction formed by conserved lysine residues in L3, substitutions of which impair viral gene expression and propagation. The dimensions and electrostatic properties of the channel are consistent with a potential role in molecular exchange across the core wall. Together, our findings establish a structural framework for understanding the organization and potential function of the poxvirus portal complex.

#739. ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Set for December Rerelease With New Scenes

Rosario Dawson's Night Nurse is among the highlights of the previously unseen footage for the extended cut, titled 'Spider-Man: [Brand New] Brand New Day.'

After a record-breaking summer, Sony Pictures is looking to soar even higher with its theatrical rerelease for Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

The studio announced Monday that the movie’s extended cut will appropriately be titled Spider-Man: [Brand New] Brand New Day and is set to return exclusively to theaters on Friday, Dec. 4. The new footage will run 10 minutes in total and feature previously unseen scenes, including one with Rosario Dawson playing the Night Nurse. The rerelease will also include a couple of other surprises that have not yet been disclosed. Related Stories Movies Johnny Depp's 'Ebenezer' Unwraps $19M to Win Weekend in Box Office Return Movies Matt Damon Reveals Ben Affleck's Review of 'The Odyssey' -- and the One Performance He Couldn't Stop Talking About

Tom Holland made his big-screen return as Peter Parker in filmmaker Destin Daniel Cretton‘s Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which was an absolute sensation upon hitting theaters July 31. It currently stands as the highest-grossing title ever at the domestic box office with $959 million, meaning that a rerelease could help push it beyond the billion-dollar mark for North America. Also starring Zendaya, Jon Bernthal, Mark Ruffalo and Sadie Sink, the movie ranks No. 3 on the all-time worldwide chart with $2.5 billion.

Also set for theatrical release on Dec. 4 are Universal’s David Harbour-led sequel Violent Night 2, the Pedro Pascal vehicle Behemoth! and Lionsgate’s Idris Elba-starring action film Above the Below. Spider-Man: Brand New Day hails from producers Marvel Studios and Amy Pascal.

The Hollywood Reporter reported back in late September that Brand New Day would be returning to theaters with previously unseen footage. That news broke days after Marvel Studios’ Avengers Endgame: Encore topped the weekend’s domestic box office, with the rerelease of the 2019 box office smash grossing $26 million to prevail over a slew of newcomers. Endgame’s rerelease was timed to drum up additional excitement for Disney’s Avengers: Doomsday, hitting theaters Dec. 18.

During a fan event in July, Dawson told the crowd that she had filmed a scene for Brand New Day as Claire Temple — the Marvel character she previously portrayed on the series Daredevil, Jessica Jones, Luke Cage, Iron Fist and The Defenders — but that it landed on the cutting room floor.

“My character is somewhere in that same universe, and I really love that,” the actress said at the time about her character, who is a version of the Night Nurse. “I hope I get to be Claire again.”

While speaking with THR shortly after the release of Brand New Day, Sony film chief Tom Rothman addressed the challenge of following the studio’s previous Spidey movie, 2021’s Spider-Man: No Way Home, which featured the high-profile returns of previous Peter Parkers in Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield.

“The strategic decision was — rather than trying what we all thought would be perhaps an empty effort of going quote, unquote bigger — we just went deeper,” Rothman explained. “That was a very conscious choice to focus on how we could make the audience feel.”

"That was the holy grail of spaceflight."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential.

Starship launched on its 15th test flight on Friday evening (Nov. 13), rising into the sky from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. The mission plan called for bringing both of the vehicle's stages back to Starbase and catching them with the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — an unprecedented total recovery of an orbital rocket.

That didn't happen; Starship's Super Heavy booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship succeeded in its attempt, notching a huge milestone for SpaceX and its dream of full rocket reuse.

"That was the missing link," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast today, his voice thick with emotion. "That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

The Ship catch occurred today at 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT; 3:20 p.m. local Texas time), roughly 22.5 hours after Flight 15 lifted off.

Many SpaceX employees went outside to watch the vehicle, known as Ship 42, descend through the clouds toward its Starbase launch tower, which the company calls "Mechazilla."

And they got quite a show: Ship 42 nestled gently into Mechazilla's waiting arms, while "Baby Come Back" played over SpaceX's landing webcast.

"This is so incredible to see," SpaceX's Jessie Anderson said during the livestream. "One of the most incredible and historic engineering feats of all time has just happened right in front of our eyes."

Why was this such a big deal? SpaceX had already caught Super Heavy — on three previous Starship test flights, in fact. But it had never tried before with Ship. The upper stage is a tougher target, for it flies higher, farther and faster than the booster. Indeed, on Flight 15, Ship 42 came all the way back down from orbit.

While the double-catch attempt, and the chopsticks success with Ship, were Flight 15's main headlines, the mission had other objectives as well. One was getting Ship to orbit, which had happened on just one previous Starship launch — Flight 14, which lifted off on Sept. 28.

Ship deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 broadband satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO) on Flight 14, and it did so again on Flight 15. These 52 spacecraft are the first members of a constellation that will eventually consist of 100,000 satellites, if all goes according to SpaceX's plan.

Some of those Starlink satellites took video and images of Ship 42's heat shield to check its health for today's landing attempt. Those images, combined with ground-based cameras, found Ship 42 to be in good shape and ready for its big moment.

SpaceX plans to use Starship to build an even bigger network in LEO than the Starlink V3 system — Starmind, an AI data-center constellation that will harbor a million spacecraft, according to Elon Musk. (For context: SpaceX's current-gen Starlink network employs about 11,000 satellites at the moment.)

Assembling these megaconstellations will require an incredible launch cadence. The double chopstick catch is key to that vision, SpaceX says, for it will enable quicker inspection, refurbishment and reflight of Starship.

So the company will doubtless try the maneuver again soon — probably on the next Starship flight, which won't be too far down the road.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 8 a.m. EST to include new details on SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 mission from SpaceX. Space.com Editor-in-Chief Tariq Malik contributed to this report. It was updated again at 4:45 p.m. ET on Nov. 14 with news of successful Ship catch.

#737. The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved

Long before a mammal is born, its skin begins establishing the precise locations where hair will eventually grow. These developing hair follicles form intricate geometric arrangements that differ from species to species. But what determines where each follicle appears, and how does the body create such orderly patterns?

Researchers at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) have identified a surprisingly simple process that may help explain this biological mystery. By studying how cells move in response to chemical signals, the team developed a model that successfully recreates the formation of hair follicle patterns in two mammalian species. Their findings, published in PNAS, suggest that elaborate biological structures can emerge naturally from basic interactions between neighboring cells.

The discovery could help explain a much broader phenomenon in nature. Hair, feathers, and most types of scales begin as small structures called placodes that appear during embryonic development. Scientists have spent decades investigating how these early structures establish the distinctive arrangements seen across different animal species.

Challenging a Long-Standing Theory of Hair Growth

For laboratory mice (Mus musculus), the leading explanation has traditionally been the expansion-induction model. This theory proposes that when a new placode appears, it releases a chemical that prevents additional placodes from developing too close to it.

As the embryo's skin grows and stretches, some areas move far enough away from existing placodes to escape the chemical's influence. New placodes can then develop in those spaces, gradually creating a more complete pattern across the skin.

Although this explanation has gained widespread acceptance, scientists have not experimentally established that it can account for the diversity of follicle patterns found across species.

A Simpler Mechanism for Hair Follicle Formation

To investigate another possibility, researchers led by Athanasia Tzika, Senior Lecturer, and Michel Milinkovitch, Professor, both in the Department of Genetics and Evolution at UNIGE's Faculty of Science, focused on a process called chemotaxis.

Chemotaxis occurs when cells move in response to differences in chemical concentrations. The same basic process helps guide white blood cells toward areas of inflammation, allowing the immune system to respond where it is needed.

The researchers created a mathematical model that tracks how mobile cells in the dermis interact with an attracting chemical signal released by the epidermis, the skin's outer layer. They then simulated the growth of embryonic skin to see whether these interactions could produce the gradual appearance of placodes.

Remarkably, the model recreated the developmental patterns observed in laboratory mice, including the same sequence of follicle formation that scientists had previously explained using the expansion-induction theory. This suggests that a complex system of instructions may not be necessary to determine where follicles develop.

"Our findings show that the observed patterns do not require a complex system telling each placode where to form," explain Muhamet Ibrahimi and Ebrahim Jahanbakhsh, researchers in the Department of Genetics and Evolution. "Instead, placodes emerge spontaneously from local interactions between cells and chemical signals."

One Simple Process Creates Different Hair Patterns

The team next investigated whether the same mechanism could explain follicle arrangements in another mammal with a very different coat structure.

They selected the spiny mouse (Acomys dimidiatus), a rodent whose hair follicles develop in an unusually regular pattern with a strong directional alignment. This distinctive organization cannot be explained by the traditional expansion-induction model.

Using experimental information gathered from three-dimensional images of developing embryonic skin, the researchers adapted their simulations to reflect the spiny mouse's particular biochemical characteristics and the way its skin grows.

The results showed that the same underlying process of cells responding to chemical signals could also reproduce the spiny mouse's highly organized follicle pattern. The differences between the two species could be explained by variations in their cellular interactions, chemical properties, and skin growth rather than entirely different mechanisms.

These findings suggest that the remarkable variety of structures found throughout the animal kingdom may arise from a shared set of relatively simple biological rules. By adjusting how cells interact and respond to their surroundings, nature can generate dramatically different patterns without requiring a separate developmental blueprint for every species.

"Our work suggests that simple cellular interactions can generate the remarkable diversity of tissue architectures observed throughout evolution," concludes Athanasia Tzika. "The differences observed between species therefore result from the same self-organization process, but with variations in the interactions between cells and chemical signals."

#736. Rob Riggle Saw ‘Nickels’ As a Way to Branch Out from Comedy

Riggle and director Spencer King discuss the drama, about a man who comes to believe a neighbor may be the reincarnated spirit of his late brother.

For Rob Riggle, Nickels was a chance to show off another color in his performing palette. The actor is known for his comedy chops, with scene stealing work in the Jump Street movies and Step Brothers, but in the new film, he plays a man who has long grieved the death of his brother in a motorcycle crash decades earlier. After a college-aged neighbor Mitch (Aaron Holliday) has his own motorcycle accident, Riggle’s character, Tom Monroe, starts to wonder if this young man has become a reincarnation of his brother. There are similiarities too eery to miss, though the audience could interpret it a number of ways, including perhaps the neighbor is misleaidng Tom. Related Stories Movies 'Jimmy' Review: KJ Apa Tries, in Vain, to Save Ploddingly Dutiful James Stewart Biopic Movies 'The Wilderness' Filmmaker Spencer King Signs with Rewind Artists (Exclusive)

The film took shape thanks to another Tom — Briarcliff boss Tom Ortenberg, who got ahold of the script from Tim Tuchrello and approached director Spencer King, who’d grown up with Ordenberg’s son. From there, Ortenberg suggested Riggle for the lead, and the actor signed on after a Zoom with King, who beamed in from a truck stop in Utah, where he was working on his previous movie, The Wilderness.

Over a quick 19 days, King and Riggle filmed the movie around Los Angeles, with Odessa A’zion playing Riggle’s onscreen daughter and Elizabeth Tulloch also starring as his wife. After a theatrical release last month, the film is available on PVOD via Briarcliff.

Rob, you’ve been on a lot of sets. Was there anything unusual about this experience?

ROB RIGGLE When you shoot a film that’s on a tight on schedule, there’s just no time to screw around. You’ve got to focus. And that’s why having a director that has a vision and knows what he or she wants to grab is a must-have before you can move to the next setup. Spencer brings that level of confidence to the set.

SPENCER KING It’s also why you need a lead actor who is an ex-Marine. Keep everyone in line. (Laughs.)

As a guy with a beard, I appreciated yours here, Rob. Whose choice was that?

RIGGLE I think it was my girlfriend’s idea. And then I got it approved by Spencer. That also just cuts down on makeup time a lot.

There’s a potential supernatural element here. Spencer, did you have a dial in your head of how far you wanted to take it?

KING For me, it’s a film where you can kind of bring your own faith into it. You can bring your own perspectives on the world and your own spirituality. The film isn’t trying to convince you of thinking any differently. For me, the interesting tidbit was not, is he the brother or is he not? It’s, does he believe he’s the brother? Or does Mitch believe he’s Tom’s brother? Or is he messing him?

Rob, you got to shoot this at home in L.A. How often have you shot in L.A. over the last decade?

RIGGLE It probably has been over a decade. I’ve shot some television here, but as far as a feature film, it might have been the Catalina wine mixer [from 2008’s Step Brothers]. It’d been awhile. You can’t put a price tag on being able to go sleep in your own bed every night. It’s a really special deal. So I consider myself incredibly lucky that we got to do that here.

Anytime you make a movie on this scale, you’ve got to call in favors. What were some of those you called in to make this owrk?

KING Equipment-wise, we called in every favor. Luke Dyra, our DP, called in all the favors and we pulled a lot of post favors.

RIGGLE Producers were also doing a lot of outreach. They were working the phones all the time. They were like, “All right, we got this location. All right, we got this motorcycle. Oh, we got this spot.” They were cooking with gas the whole time.

KING For me, this was, this is one of my favorite types of movies. It’s something Rob and I talked about in the production of it. A lot of my favorite movies are when more comedic actors go serious. Eternal Sunshine is one of my favorite movies. Adam Sandler’s done it a handful of times, Will Ferrell and Stranger Than Fiction, and I really thought this was one of those. This has a chance to be that for Rob in a lot of ways. Not that Rob hasn’t done it, but it’s such a different look. I think that sometimes comedians are building up to a punchline. So there’s a natural sequence for working up to a crescendo of sorts. What I felt on set and in the edit was Rob naturally was able to pinpoint the inflection point of the scene and in some sort of subtle way be able to deliver that scene’s “punchline.”

RIGGLE Well, you’re very kind to say that. I think comedic actors, myself included, the reason we get to keep doing comedies is because hopefully we do them well. But it’s like a palette of colors. I’ve got a lot of colors on the palette. Everybody’s seen red. I can do that, but I got other colors. I can do green, I can do yellow, I can do blue, whatever you want. I think a lot of actors, especially comedy actors, don’t get the opportunities. So that’s another reason I was so grateful to be part of this.

#735. What Germany thinks of carmaker Audi's $4 billion deal with Trump

The luxury carmaker is set to open its first factory in the United States — a move Trump credits to his tariffs. DW examines the German reaction amid a massive auto industry cull at home.

US President Donald Trump announced the investment on Saturday, during a campaign rally in Georgia, a key battleground state for his Republican Party in the midterm elections next week.

Audi quickly confirmed the plan, saying it would build its first US factory near Macon, Georgia, costing around $4 billion (€3.6 billion) and creating some 4,500 jobs.

The German automaker said construction would begin next year, with a planned annual production of up to 200,000 vehicles due to start in the early 2030s.

The firm plans to build premium SUVs for the US market at the plant, marking a "long-term commitment" to what it said was "one of the world's most important premium markets."

The US investment comes as German automakers face unprecedented pressure from China, rising costs and two conflicts.

Backed by huge government subsidies, Chinese rivals have stolen a march in the transition to electric vehicles (EVs), scaling up production of new models that are fast gaining market share in a crowded global auto market.

BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Audi's parent company, Volkswagen— the world's second-largest automaker — have all issued profit warnings in recent months as margins come under pressure.

They've also announced major cost-cutting. VW is preparing to axe up to 100,000 jobs by 2030, while Audi's factory in Neckarsulm, which has around 15,000 staff, is one of four plants at risk of closure.

Trump credited his 15% tariffs on European-made vehicles for Audi's investment, saying it "would not have happened without tariffs."

While the commitment does feed into Trump's plan to bring manufacturing back to the United States from abroad, Audi said it was making the huge outlay for growth and resilience.

“We have much greater ambitions for Audi in America," said the carmaker's CEO Gernot Döllner, who appeared alongside Trump at the Republican's campaign rally.

"The United States is one of the world's most important premium markets, and we have not yet realized our full potential. We are determined to change that ... This is about building a stronger Audi business in America — not only about building a factory," he said.

However, Trump's tariffs have undoubtedly added to the automaker's woes.

Audi, which currently exports to the US market from Europe and Mexico, said the additional costs amounted to about €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion) last year.

With more than 160,000 vehicles sold, Audi's US sales last year fell 16%, amid intense competition and after Trump scrapped subsidies on electric vehicles in its second-biggest market.

By building a US factory, Audi should be able to avoid or reduce Trump's tariffs, industry analysts say.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

There's been fierce criticism of the deal due to the severe pressure facing German automakers and because the new US investment could mean further job losses at home.

Much of the criticism focused on Döllner's rally appearance alongside Trump.

The center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD)'s transport policy spokesperson Isabel Cademartori described it as campaign assistance for an autocrat who is waging a trade war against Germany.

"This is a disgrace, especially considering the history of the Volkswagen Group," she stated, referring to the company's links with Adolf Hitler's Nazi party during World War II.

Christiane Benner, president of the powerful IG Metall union, labeled the rally appearance as "extremely embarrassing, politically unacceptable and not worthy of the company."

VW works council chief Daniela Cavallo went further, saying Döllner had let himself be turned "into a puppet in [Trump's] propaganda show."

Cavallo, however, noted that the US plant could make sense from a business perspective, as VW needs to grow its market share there.

An Audi spokesperson defended the US investment, saying it was "not a decision against Germany, but rather a step toward strengthening our global competitiveness."

Manfred Döss, chairman of Audi's supervisory board, insisted the automaker's future cannot be secured by cost-cutting and efficiency alone.

"We need the courage to invest, to seize new opportunities and to make decisions that will shape our company for decades to come," he added.

The announcement certainly appears timed to coincide with the US midterm elections on November 3.

Voters will decide whether the Republicans or Democrats hold the balance of power in Congress during Trump's last two years in office.

Holding the announcement in the key battleground state of Georgia is seen as a strategic move to boost the fortunes of local Republican candidates.

Since he returned to the White House last year, Trump has used tariffs and political pressure to force global automakers to relocate their factories to American soil.

Audi's investment follows moves by Stellantis and Japan's Toyota to expand US production, while Honda is in talks to build a new US plant.

US auto giants General Motors and Ford have also promised to increase domestic production.

While one investment announcement may not be enough to sway many voters, it serves one of Trump's main election promises — to revive industrial production in the US.

#734. Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have uncovered new clues about why some people develop heart disease even after lowering their bad cholesterol to recommended levels. Their findings point to biological processes involving other fat-carrying particles in the blood that may contribute to cardiovascular damage in ways that go beyond cholesterol buildup. By identifying these previously poorly understood mechanisms, the research could help pave the way for more targeted strategies to prevent heart disease and potentially save lives.

Heart disease remains one of the world's leading causes of death. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), cardiovascular diseases kill nearly 17.9 million people worldwide each year, with heart attacks and strokes responsible for more than 80% of those deaths. Coronary heart disease develops when fatty deposits containing cholesterol (cholesterol) build up inside the arteries that supply blood to the heart. If left untreated, the condition can eventually cause a heart attack.

Reducing LDL cholesterol, commonly known as "bad cholesterol," is a proven way to lower the likelihood of a heart attack. However, bringing LDL cholesterol into the recommended range does not eliminate the danger. Some patients continue to develop coronary heart disease despite successful treatment, suggesting that other particles transporting fats through the bloodstream play an important role. Until recently, the biological reasons behind this remaining risk were not well understood.

"For this study, we wanted to understand what happens beyond the accumulation of cholesterol in artery walls, whether different fat-carrying particles can damage the blood vessels differently and why the remaining risk of heart disease still occurs," says Jakub Morze, lead author and a postdoctoral fellow at Chalmers University of Technology, in Sweden.

Cholesterol is a substance similar to fat that circulates in the bloodstream. The body needs it to build cells and manufacture certain vitamins and hormones. Problems can arise when too much cholesterol accumulates in blood vessel walls, creating deposits called plaques.

These plaques can narrow arteries and interfere with blood flow. If a plaque ruptures, a blood clot may form quickly and completely obstruct the affected vessel, potentially triggering a heart attack or stroke.

Because cholesterol and other fats cannot travel through the blood on their own, they are transported by specialized particles known as lipoproteins. Three major classes of these particles contain a surface protein called apolipoprotein B (apoB). When too many of these particles circulate in the blood, they can deliver excess cholesterol into artery walls. The cholesterol they carry is commonly referred to as "bad cholesterol."

To investigate these unanswered questions, the scientists used proteomics analysis to examine how three types of fat-carrying particles (LDL, TRL and Lp(a)) affect the body and may contribute to heart disease. This approach allowed the team to investigate biological changes associated with the particles rather than focusing exclusively on the cholesterol they carry.

All three types can contribute to cholesterol deposits inside artery walls, although LDL, which stands for low-density lipoprotein, is the most common. In a previous study, the same research group found that counting harmful lipoprotein particles was the most effective way to predict future heart disease risk.

The researchers also identified two particularly important contributors beyond LDL: triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, or TRL, and lipoprotein(a), known as Lp(a). Their earlier findings suggested that each of these particles poses a greater risk individually than an LDL particle. As a result, TRL and Lp(a) are considered major contributors to the cardiovascular danger that can persist even after LDL cholesterol has been successfully reduced.

Proteomics is the systematic, large-scale examination and measurement of proteins within cells, tissues, or body fluids at a particular point in time.

While genomics investigates a person's relatively stable DNA, proteomics focuses on proteins, which are constantly responding to changes inside the body. These molecules help construct tissues, process food, transmit hormonal messages, and defend against infections.

Because protein patterns shift in response to factors such as diet, stress, aging, and disease, analyzing them can provide a snapshot of current biological activity. Proteomics can help researchers identify biomarkers, diagnose medical conditions, and track how patients respond to treatment.

Blood Proteins Reveal Hidden Heart Disease Risks

The new investigation focused on proteins, which perform countless essential functions throughout the body. Unlike genetic information, which remains largely unchanged, protein levels and activity can respond to diet, stress, aging, and illness. Studying these changes can therefore provide valuable insights into the body's current biological condition.

Researchers analyzed measurements of nearly 3,000 proteins found in blood samples and compared the results with genetic information and long-term health records. This combination helped them identify protein patterns associated with different lipoprotein particles and provided clues about how those particles might contribute to damage inside the arteries.

One of the most striking discoveries involved TRL and Lp(a). Although these are distinct types of particles, their associated blood protein patterns showed substantial similarities. Those overlapping patterns also appeared to be linked to the later development of heart disease.

The researchers found that these particles carried proteins capable of attracting immune cells, potentially encouraging inflammation and changes in the structure of blood vessel walls. This suggests that TRL and Lp(a) may contribute to cardiovascular disease through some of the same biological processes, rather than simply depositing cholesterol in the arteries.

LDL showed a different pattern. Its associated proteins were primarily connected to cholesterol accumulation in artery walls, highlighting an important distinction between the ways these three types of particles may contribute to heart disease.

"The overlap for TRL and Lp(a) is one of the most interesting findings," says Morze. "It suggests that these particles may affect some of the same inflammatory and vascular processes. This could help identify targets for more precisely directed prevention in the future."

How LDL, TRL, and Lp(a) Affect Heart Health

The three types of lipoproteins examined in the study, LDL, TRL, and Lp(a), transport different amounts of cholesterol and other fats through the bloodstream. Each contains the structural protein apolipoprotein B, or apoB.

All three can contribute to atherosclerosis, a condition in which fatty material accumulates inside blood vessel walls. As these deposits develop, they increase the risk of coronary heart disease.

LDL: Low-density lipoprotein transports most of the cholesterol circulating in the blood. An LDL cholesterol measurement indicates how much cholesterol is contained within these particles.

TRL: Triglyceride-rich lipoproteins transport cholesterol along with triglycerides, which the body uses as an important energy source. As triglycerides are removed from these particles, the remaining fragments can deposit cholesterol inside artery walls. In this study, the TRL measurements primarily reflected liver-produced particles called VLDL and the remnants they leave behind.

Lp(a): Lipoprotein(a) resembles an LDL particle but contains an additional protein known as apolipoprotein(a). Higher levels of Lp(a) are already recognized as an established risk factor for coronary heart disease.

Could the Discovery Lead to Better Heart Disease Prevention?

By identifying biological pathways associated with cardiovascular risk beyond LDL cholesterol, the findings offer researchers new possibilities for developing more personalized prevention strategies. In particular, the shared inflammatory and blood vessel effects linked to TRL and Lp(a) could become promising areas for further investigation.

However, the research did not evaluate a new treatment or establish a blood protein test ready for routine clinical use. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether measuring these biological processes, or developing treatments that target them, can improve protection against heart disease.

"Lowering LDL cholesterol remains a cornerstone of prevention," says Clemens Wittenbecher, who led the study and is Assistant Professor of Precision Medicine and Diagnostics at Chalmers. "Our findings point to biological processes that may help explain some of the risk that remains beyond LDL. The next step is to establish whether measuring or targeting these processes can improve prevention alongside existing treatments."

The results reinforce the importance of controlling LDL cholesterol while revealing why cholesterol reduction alone may not address every source of cardiovascular risk. Understanding the additional ways blood particles affect arteries could ultimately help scientists develop more precise approaches to protecting heart health.

The study, "Apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins: distinct roles in atherosclerosis revealed by plasma proteomic profiling," was published in the European Heart Journal.

The research authors are Jakub Morze, Elias Björnson, Michael Y Mi, Martin Adiels, Giorgio E Melloni, Gonçalo Rosas da Silva, Andrzej Rynkiewicz, Nicholas A Marston, Marta Guasch-Ferré, Michael Y Tsai, Jerome I Rotter, Robert E Gerszten, Qi Sun, Frank B Hu, Rikard Landberg, Göran Bergström, Chris J Packard, Jan Borén and Clemens Wittenbecher.

At the time of the research, the authors were affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology and the Institute of Medicine at the University of Gothenburg, Sweden; Harvard Medical School, USA; AstraZeneca, Sweden; Municipal Hospital in Olsztyn, Poland; University of Copenhagen, Denmark; University of Minnesota, USA; The Lundquist Institute at Harbour-UCLA Medical Center in Torrance, USA; Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, USA; and the University of Glasgow, UK.

#733. John Oliver Fills in for Tom Papa at Michael J. Fox Foundation Gala After FAA Ground Stop

Friday's four-hour halt to flights taking off across the U.S. also served as fodder for Josh Johnson's stand-up set, where he poked fun at last week's Microsoft outage as well.

By Saturday, air travel across the U.S. had resumed after the Federal Aviation Administration’s four-hour nationwide ground stop on Friday.

But the effects of the stoppage were still unfolding, including in the entertainment world. At Saturday night’s Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research gala in New York, host Denis Leary told the crowd that while they were fortunate that not many of the stars set to appear were affected by the ground stop, stand-up comedian Tom Papa, who was scheduled to perform at the benefit, was stuck in Los Angeles due to the grounding. Related Stories Music Grammys: Michael J. Fox, Tim Curry, 'Wicked: For Good,' 'The Pitt' Among Hollywood Nominees Lifestyle Baby2Baby Gala Fetes Demi Moore and Raises Over $20M for the Cause

In fact, he’d boarded his flight and was about to take off before the FAA ground stop on Friday.

But luckily the Michael J. Fox Foundation found another stand-up comedian in New York who could fill in: John Oliver. The Last Week Tonight host was a surprise performer at the star-studded annual benefit, where he initially joked that he was disappointing the audience after they’d already been told the scheduled comedian wasn’t coming and Leary got the crowd thinking maybe Jon Stewart would be filling in since he mentioned that Oliver knows Stewart.

The FAA flight stoppage also served as fodder for fellow stand-up and Jon Stewart associate, Josh Johnson, as the Daily Show host used the beginning of his stand-up set to poke fun at Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s reality TV past on The Real World: Boston and how the way he’d said a cyberattack wasn’t responsible for Friday’s ground stop (the FAA insisted the pause was due to air traffic control communication issues) made Johnson think it was definitely a cyberattack.

Johnson also got some mileage out of the Microsoft outage that lasted from midday Thursday into early Friday, joking that it was great for people who were bad at their jobs, because they could simply claim they sent an email that no one could check.

“This is a dream come true for a low-tier employee,” he said.

Elsewhere at the event, which raised a record-breaking $6 million, former Late Show hosts Stephen Colbert and David Letterman made separate appearances where they jokingly stressed their ongoing relevance despite their CBS late night shows coming to an end.

Colbert joked, as he introduced a video of scientists working on medical treatments for Parkinson’s as the Fox Foundation aims to find a cure for the neurodegenerative disorder, that being at the glitzy event at the Waldorf-Astoria in Manhattan made him “feel like [he has] a job.” And Letterman complimented the well-heeled audience in the hotel ballroom as he took a video on his phone to “prove to people that he’s still in show business.”

The event ended with what’s become a tradition at the gala of Fox joining the headlining musician onstage for a Back to the Future-inspired rendition of “Johnny B. Goode.” This year, Fox joined John Mayer and Brad Paisley along with No Doubt’s Tom Dumont and Shoshana Bean. And Mayer, like Chris Martin, shared that the “new sound” Fox showed off as Marty McFly had made him want to pick up a guitar when he was a kid.

At the end of the benefit, Fox grabbed the microphone and joked that being able to perform with Mayer, Paisley and others was “definitely worth having Parkinson’s for” and expressed a renewed commitment to finding a cure.

Earlier on the red carpet, Fox’s friends and former colleagues spoke about how happy they were that he’d been able to return to acting this year in Shrinking.

“When I saw the footage I said, ‘This is such a perfect pairing [of Fox and Harrison Ford’s character who has Parkinson’s], under a perfect premise,'” Leary told The Hollywood Reporter.

Fox’s former Spin City co-star Alan Ruck suggested that the work done through Fox’s foundation and improvements in Parkinson’s treatments may have contributed to him being able to act again.

“I know that the medicine has improved a lot since the year 2000, because that’s when he stepped away from Spin,” Ruck offered. “Because it wasn’t enough for him to go to work. It was debilitating. But the medicine has improved so much, now he’s on Shrinking. He’s done a number of things since then so that’s encouraging that all of this research is paying off. And through this foundation, he is helping people’s lives improve.”

And Leary, who’d worked with Fox on FX’s Rescue Me, teased that he might have another acting gig for his friend.

“I think he’s a great actor. So I jealously always want to create a character for him in whatever I’m doing. So I’m actually thinking about creating a character for him in this next thing I’m going to do,” Leary told THR.

Other stars who attended the event included Christopher Lloyd, Clark Gregg, Ted McGinley, Susie Essman, Ali Wentworth, George Stephanopoulos, Willie Geist and Terry Crews, whose wife Rebecca King Crews has been living with Parkinson’s, going public with her diagnosis earlier this year.

The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program.

The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad, commander, and Alan Bean, the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon, the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms.

The previous moon mission, Apollo 11, drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3. Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier.

The Apollo 12 moonwalkers also performed a lot of moon science. The astronauts picked up 75 pounds of moon rocks. Most of the rocks were basalts that formed from molten lava. These basalts showed the Apollo 12 landing site is more than 3 billion years old.

Apollo 12 proved that the Apollo 11 moon landing was not just a one-off stunt while setting the stage for even more ambitious missions.

To truly explore the moon and advance our understanding of how our solar system formed, the follow-on Apollo flights needed to be able to land where the geologists had identified as areas of interest. Apollo 12, with its touchdown in proximity to the Surveyor probe, proved this was possible.

The launch of Apollo 12 also underscored the importance of having a well-prepared Mission Control team, an asset that would be critical to outcome of the next mission, Apollo 13.

The ability to recover from a complete electrical short out with the simple call of a through of a switch "SCE to AUX" proved that knowing every detail about how the spacecraft worked was key to a successful program. #731. At Least Robert Pattinson Looks the Part…According to Ian Fleming

The Bond author commissioned a sketch of 007 in the 1950s — and it bears an uncanny resemblance to a certain British actor currently being fitted for a tuxedo.

Well, it took nearly 70 years, and there were plenty of detours along the way, but Ian Fleming finally got the James Bond of his dreams — at least when it comes to jawline and nose shape.

None of the previous 007s — not Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan, or even Daniel Craig — looked anything like how the character’s creator envisioned him. In Fleming’s mind — at least according to the SMERSH dossier occasionally referred to in his books — Bond was about six-foot tall, 168 pounds, with black hair and blue eyes. For Pattison, that’s check, check, check and check. But for the actors who proceeded him, not so much. Related Stories Movies James Bond Fans Already Complaining About Robert Pattinson: "Not Alpha Male" Movies How 'Twilight' Predicted Robert Pattinson's James Bond Casting

Connery and Lazenby had dark hair but brown eyes. Craig had blue eyes but fair hair (controversial coloring that inspired more than a few cheeky headlines when he was cast: “No Mr. Blonde, They Expect You To Dye”). Moore had blue eyes but his hair was shades too light. Brosnan came closest, with black hair and blue eyes. But it turns out Fleming had other criteria aside from basic coloring and measurements.

In fact, the author commissioned a portrait of Bond in the 1950s, years before the movies were launched, when a British newspaper purchased the rights to serialize the novels as a cartoon strip. To help the paper’s illustrator nail down the look, Fleming hired an unknown artist to sketch 007’s face according to his highly specific instructions (“I think we should avoid giving Bond an American-shaped head and a duck’s haircut,” he wrote in one note).

The result was a long angular face with heavy brows, a narrow nose, sharp cheekbones, thin lips and a firm, squared-off chin that looks uncannily like… Robert Pattinson.

The funny thing is, the newspaper’s illustrator, John McLusky, pretty much ignored Fleming’s ideas and drew his own Bond with a much more rugged appearance — narrower eyes, a more expansive jawline, and a broad, cleft chin. In other words, a face that looked uncannily like… Sean Connery, who’d be cast in the part a half-decade later.
